Following Trump's election as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. After the new US administration takes office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two respects — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have profound implications for the global economic landscape. It is worth noting that, amid an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes, a strengthening US dollar, and the possibility of the US adopting trade protectionist measures, the risks faced by emerging market economies have intensified somewhat. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained largely stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates rose alongside US dollar interbank rates. Nevertheless, liquidity conditions remained sound, and overall loan growth rose further in the second half of 2016. Following the introduction of the new stamp duty measure, the residential property market showed immediate signs of adjustment, but has recovered somewhat recently. Looking ahead, banks should carefully assess the possibility that the pace of US interest rate hikes may be faster than expected, as well as the impact of broader US policy uncertainty, particularly the risk of large-scale capital outflows and its potential impact on local interest rates.  Following Trump's election as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Not only was the election outcome beyond market expectations, but the related market reaction was also surprising. In particular, expectations that Trump's tax reforms, increased infrastructure spending, and deregulation measures would boost US economic growth drove global equity markets higher. After the new US administration takes office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two respects — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have profound implications for the global economic landscape. However, the tax cut measures that the market anticipates from Trump may fail to deliver the expected stimulus to US economic growth. In particular, with US economic activity now close to its economic potential, fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a mild cyclical boost to US economic growth, while exacerbating the upside risks to US inflation. Although it remains uncertain whether the US Federal Reserve (the Fed) will therefore significantly accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening, long-term bond yields have risen markedly, partly reflecting market expectations of rising inflation risks. At the same time, rising trade protectionism would create a "lose-lose" situation for the US and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions that harm overall interests, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Meanwhile, political instability remains a major risk and adverse factor, particularly for the still fragile European economic recovery.  For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows arising from an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar has already risen. This could weigh on economic growth and heighten the risk of rapid capital outflows. Indeed, amid expectations that the Trump administration will pursue large-scale fiscal expansion and concerns over surging energy prices, the market has already repriced inflation risks, causing long-term bond yields to rise significantly across the board in advanced economies as well as in a number of emerging market economies. Box 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. The findings show that, since the 2013 "taper tantrum", the influence of the US Treasury bond market on sovereign bond markets has deepened, and that US interest rate hikes and tightening financial conditions would have a significant impact on both advanced economies and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016 as exports recovered, but the earlier market volatility — including regional currency depreciation and rising sovereign bond yields driven by concerns over possible policy changes by the incoming US administration — only gradually stabilised early this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain steady growth in 2017, but the risks and uncertainties it faces have both risen. US interest rate hikes, regional currency depreciation, and heightened financial market volatility may lead to tightening financial conditions. At the same time, the US may pursue protectionist policies, which could affect regional economies, though the actual impact remains unclear for now.  In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated marginally in the second half of 2016 amid robust growth in infrastructure investment and improving private sector business spending. Although the economy continued to show signs of stabilisation, uncertainties remain in the Mainland's growth outlook. In particular, with the government determined to curb rising property prices, if the property market continues to cool, the property sector's contribution to growth this year may diminish. At the same time, the ongoing advancement of economic structural adjustment and changes in Sino-US trade relations may increase uncertainty in the near-term economic outlook. On the external front, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) currency basket during the review period, capital outflow pressure increased somewhat towards the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate hikes, and subsequently appeared to ease slightly in early 2017. Although private sector economic activity showed signs of stabilisation, some concerns remained in the market over the effectiveness of monetary policy, particularly given that M1 growth has been accelerating while M2 growth has slowed. Box 2 (see page 24) examines whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, while Box 3 (see page 27) examines the factors that may have caused the divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The findings indicate that there is no evidence that the Mainland has fallen into a liquidity trap, and that the main reasons for M1 growing markedly faster than M2 are that the monetary easing of recent years has reduced the opportunity cost of holding liquid money, and that rising economic uncertainty may have increased the demand for precautionary money.  Hong Kong's economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016. Quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Domestically, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while buoyant infrastructure activity in the fourth quarter drove investment growth. Externally, goods export growth rose as regional trade flows improved, while services exports grew steadily amid a recovery in trade-related and transport services. As growth in imports of goods and services was faster, net exports continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half of the year. As economic growth picked up, the overall unemployment rate edged down to 3.3% in December. Economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. The government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2017 are 2-3% and 2.0% respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook still faces significant external headwinds. The protectionist rhetoric of the incoming US administration has increased downside risks to global trade as well as to Hong Kong's external demand. Amid upward pressure on the US dollar and expectations of an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes, the global financial environment is expected to provide less support to the real economy, and could lead to tighter local financial conditions, particularly in the event of tail risks. Box 4 (see page 41) discusses the compilation of Hong Kong's Financial Conditions Index to help monitor local financial conditions.  Since the second half of 2016, local inflationary pressure has remained moderate, while quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum accelerated slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly due to volatility in food prices and rising housing rentals. With stable import prices and moderate local cost pressures, inflationary pressure is expected to remain manageable. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained largely stable, but weakened at times after the US interest rate hike in December. The Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. As the US dollar appreciated, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate rose further. Owing to the large Monetary Base, Hong Kong interbank interest rates remained low, but have risen since October due to year-end funding demand and catching up with the rise in US dollar interest rates. As a result, the average mortgage rate, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in the mortgage lending business, edged up to 2.07% in January 2017.  Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared with growth of 2.2% in the first half. Growth was supported by strengthening local economic activity and rising financing demand from multinational corporations around year-end. Local loan growth accelerated slightly, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after a slight decline in the first half. By currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans recorded growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced repayments of foreign currency loans. Banks' funding positions remained largely sound. The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down to 77.1% at the end of 2016, reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 59.9% at year-end, while the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio dropped markedly to 63.8% owing to strong growth in US dollar deposits.  Owing to the strength of the US dollar, both onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi funding pool (comprising customer deposits and certificate of deposit balances) underwent further consolidation, as did other offshore renminbi markets, and the volatility of offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank interest rates increased markedly. Nevertheless, banks' renminbi liquidity management remained sound, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is likely to continue facing headwinds arising from uncertainty over the renminbi exchange rate trend.  As global market conditions improved, the Hong Kong stock market closed substantially higher during the review period. Although the US presidential election produced an unexpected outcome, the market was only briefly affected. This was mainly due to investors' optimism over the Trump administration's fiscal stimulus measures, which drove global stock markets higher. Although benefiting from this, the local market, while optimistic, was also cautious, possibly due to concerns over an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes, challenges to the Mainland economic outlook, uncertainty over renminbi policy, and controls on capital flows. Looking ahead, although the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuation could provide support to the market.  Although Hong Kong dollar bond yields rose rapidly at the end of last year and the spread over US Treasury bonds widened sharply, the Hong Kong dollar bond market continued to expand steadily during the review period. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi bond market recovered in the second half after contracting in the first half of 2016, but new bond issuance for the full year still declined from the previous year. Looking ahead, if global investors reverse their earlier yield-seeking investment strategies, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets would come under pressure. As US trade policy remains unclear and the renminbi exchange rate may remain volatile, the outlook for both bond markets over the next half year will remain beset by significant uncertainties.  After the government introduced new stamp duty measures, the residential property market showed immediate signs of adjustment, but has recovered somewhat recently. In view of renewed market exuberance, the government raised the stamp duty to a flat rate of 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets fell in the following two months. However, transaction volumes have risen recently, partly reflecting an increase in developers' launches of primary residential projects. Meanwhile, property prices continued to rise to new highs, though the pace of increase has slowed somewhat.

Following Trump's unexpected election as US President, uncertainty surrounding US policies has increased. Although market attention has focused on the short-term benefits arising from the potential implementation of large-scale fiscal policies and business-friendly measures, US economic activity is currently close to its economic potential, and fiscal stimulus measures may only bring a mild cyclical boost to US economic growth, while further intensifying the upside risks to inflation. More importantly, the risks facing emerging market economies are increasing amid capital outflow pressures brought about by the faster pace of US interest rate hikes and a strengthening US dollar, while potential US trade protectionist measures also threaten global trade flows. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, and export volumes have recently increased. However, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, a rising US dollar, and possible US protectionist measures, financial markets should continue to be volatile, with rising downside risks to economic growth. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated marginally in the second half of 2016, supported by robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved business spending in the private sector. The Mainland economy continued to rebalance, with the tertiary sector expanding steadily, but the ongoing advancement of economic restructuring and changes in Sino-US trade relations may add to the uncertainty in the near-term economic outlook. With the government determined to curb rising property prices, if the property market continues to cool, the property sector's contribution to economic growth may also decline this year. On the external front, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 as the US dollar strengthened and US interest rates rose, and subsequently appeared to ease slightly in early 2017. Following Trump's unexpected election as US President, global financial markets reacted strongly, particularly as markets anticipated that policies such as tax reform, large-scale increases in infrastructure spending, and deregulation pursued by Trump would boost US economic growth and inflation, spurring major stock markets higher (Chart 2.1). As a result, market expectations of US inflation and US interest rate hikes intensified, sending US Treasury bond yields sharply higher and strengthening the US dollar. Chart 2.1 Stock market indices of selected advanced economies. However, the tax cut measures markets anticipated from Trump may not produce the positive impact on US economic growth that the market expects. Although a shift in economic policy towards reliance on fiscal easing measures would help relieve the heavy burden borne by monetary easing policy, given the current stage of the US economic cycle, whether now is the appropriate time to implement fiscal easing measures is debatable. Although US economic growth has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap has gradually narrowed, and the unemployment rate in February was in line with the Federal Reserve's estimated natural unemployment rate of 4.7%, reflecting that US economic activity is close to its economic potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary cycle, and the fiscal multiplier would be lower than during a recession (see, for example, Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012))1. In fact, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labour or capital may result in reduced tax revenue (see, for example, Trabandt and Uhlig (2012))2. In any case, with excess capacity diminishing, any further measures to boost economic growth—even with limited real impact on growth—may push up inflation. At the same time, other factors such as rising oil and commodity prices, as well as potential trade protectionist measures including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, may also intensify the upside risks to US inflation. Even as the risk of rising US inflation increases, the Federal Reserve has remained cautious about tightening US monetary policy and has tended to maintain an ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have already risen, partly reflecting the increased inflation risk in the US. Since the US election, although market forecasts for future federal funds rates have been revised upward to close to the median of the Federal Reserve's projections for 2017 and early 2018, they remain well below the Federal Reserve's long-term forecasts (Chart 2.2). As a result, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes could trigger the risk of significant market volatility. Although financial markets have focused on the short-term benefits arising from the potential implementation of expansionary fiscal policies and business-friendly measures that would drive stronger US economic growth, long-term risks persist, including damaging protectionist trade policies and further increases in US government debt. In fact, the Trump administration may fulfil its campaign promises and adopt trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions that harm the collective interest, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Chart 2.2 Future federal funds rate forecasts: Federal Reserve versus market. In Europe, political instability remains the primary risk and drag on Europe's economic recovery. Although the economic environment in the euro area has gradually improved, with fourth-quarter real GDP growing moderately by 1.7% year on year—only slightly below the 1.8% year-on-year increase in the third quarter—economic activity in the euro area remains only slightly above pre-global financial crisis levels compared with the stronger recovery in the US economy (Chart 2.3). Since the UK's decision to leave the EU last summer, markets have been concerned that the euro area could eventually disintegrate. Although Italy's economic and political situation appears to have stabilised after the formation of a new government and the implementation of bank rescue measures, against the backdrop of Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment, the upcoming elections in Germany and France (possibly along with Italy) could become political flashpoints. Partly due to increased political uncertainty, sovereign bond yields in Europe have continued to climb, and corporate bond spreads have widened, a situation especially evident in peripheral countries, which could create a vicious cycle affecting the real economy and may put pressure on real business investment in the euro area. Chart 2.3 Real GDP of major advanced economies. In Japan, real GDP has been revised upward in recent quarters, with the annual growth rate in the fourth quarter of 2016 rising to 1.6% year on year—the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015—and the economic recovery being stronger than previously anticipated. However, partly due to structural problems in the labour market, wage growth has been slow, resulting in weak consumption growth. At the same time, the recent rapid depreciation of the yen means that the downside pressure on "new core" goods inflation caused by the earlier appreciation of the yen is about to begin to ease. Coupled with a stronger-than-expected recovery, this indicates an improved near-term inflation outlook, and although "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy) fell to 0.1% in December, it is expected to bottom out and rebound. Nevertheless, in the face of long-term and structural headwinds, growth may remain slow, and inflation expectations remain at around 0.5%–0.6%, below the level at the time Abenomics was launched in early 2014, so the risk remains that the inflation rate may fail to reach the Bank of Japan's medium-term target of 2%. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, the benefits derived through the trade channel from faster US economic growth may be smaller, since the US has reduced its imports since the global financial crisis and the US may implement protectionist policies. At the same time, the faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar will lead to tighter financial conditions, intensifying downside economic risks. This could weigh on economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, markets have repriced inflation risks in anticipation of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration, coupled with concerns over surging energy prices, causing long-term bond yields to rise significantly across the board in advanced economies as well as in a number of emerging market economies. Box 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. In East Asia3, real economic activity has recently regained momentum, with GDP in the region growing modestly and inflation rising. Real GDP growth — In the second half of 2016, economic growth generally remained stable due to steady private consumption in a number of regional economies. At the same time, exports generally rose modestly from their 2015 lows. This benefited not only from the stabilisation of China's growth but also from improved performance in advanced economies such as the US and Europe. For net commodity exporters (such as Malaysia and Indonesia), the recovery in commodity prices provided an additional boost. Other major exporters (such as South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore) also regained upward momentum thanks to growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — As commodity prices (especially oil) recovered, producer price inflation generally showed an upward trend. Although this will push up industrial costs and even consumer spending, consumption and investment growth may increase as the risk of prolonged deflation declines. Faster producer price inflation may create upward pressure on consumer price inflation, with the actual impact depending on the extent to which the rise in producer prices is passed through to consumer prices, which varies across economies. Consensus forecasts of consumer price indices indicate that inflation in a number of regional economies, while still slightly below central banks' 2017 inflation targets, will rise closer to target levels (Chart 2.4). Apart from Indonesia, central banks in East Asia have generally kept their accommodative monetary policy on interest rates unchanged, while Indonesia cut rates twice—in September and October last year—to boost growth. Chart 2.4 Headline CPI inflation, forecasts, and central bank targets in East Asia. Despite the improvement in the real economy, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 triggered short-term volatility in financial markets. Foreign exchange market — Following the US presidential election, investors expected US inflation to rise, and most currencies in the region depreciated against the US dollar. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some currencies in the region depreciated less, or even appreciated slightly, following the US election (Chart 2.5). Chart 2.5 Post-US-election spot foreign exchange depreciation against the US dollar and changes in the nominal effective exchange rate. Bond and stock markets — Asset prices briefly fell following the US presidential election but soon stabilised. The spreads between sovereign bonds of East Asian economies and US Treasury bonds widened. However, as markets stabilised, yields in some regional economies declined, but had yet to return to pre-election levels (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, spreads have narrowed compared with pre-election levels. Chart 2.6 Spreads between 10-year sovereign bonds and US Treasury bonds. Portfolio investment flows — Portfolio investment funds flowed out of East Asia in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the "taper tantrum" in mid-2013. Inflows were recorded again in the first few weeks of 2017, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, growth in the region is expected to remain stable, but still below its historical average. With increased uncertainty over US government policies and the Federal Reserve's possible policy responses, financial markets are likely to remain volatile. A significant rise in the US dollar and yields could attract funds from the region to the US, leading investors to reduce their holdings of regional assets, which is particularly worrying for assets that are already highly valued. Tighter financial conditions in this context would also put repayment pressure on corporations that carry large amounts of US dollar-denominated debt. From a macro perspective, a broad-based rise in global interest rates would also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, which would not only weigh on aggregate demand in the short term but could also affect potential growth in the long run. Finally, exporters in the region face the potential threat of trade protectionist policies pursued by the new US administration. The US trade deficit with East Asian economies has continued to widen in recent years (Chart 2.7), particularly in the region's major export industries, such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, apparel, and textiles. Over the past two decades, US imports in these industries have increased, with substantial job losses. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalising US manufacturing could pose significant risks to exporters in the region.

Accelerated growth in private consumption and buoyant public-sector building and construction activities drove Hong Kong's economic growth to pick up slightly in the second half of 2016. Given the increasingly uncertain external environment, economic growth in 2017 is expected to be moderate. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate local growth momentum, inflationary pressure is expected to remain under control. Hong Kong's economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth rate in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly due to improved consumer confidence and a robust labour market, private consumption grew at a faster pace, becoming the main driver of GDP growth. Supported by infrastructure projects such as the Three-Runway System at Hong Kong airport, building and construction activities also became buoyant. However, owing to weak corporate capital expenditure, the contribution of overall investment expenditure to GDP growth narrowed. On the external front, both exports and imports of goods accelerated in line with rising intra-regional trade flows (Chart 3.2).²² Trade-related and transport services drove a further increase in exports of services, while imports of services rebounded partly due to strong travel demand from local residents. Net exports continued to drag on GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports The labour market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stayed at 3.4% in the first three quarters, then edged down slightly to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). In fact, the unemployment rates in several major industries declined in the second half of the year, including the retail, accommodation and food services sectors, partly because the slowdown in the retail sector had stabilised. Total employment reached a new high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labour force participation rate held steady at around 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment rate and total employment Real economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. On external factors, given the uncertainties in the global macroeconomic and financial environment, global economic and trade growth may remain moderate. Coupled with the strength of the US dollar pushing up the real effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar, this will restrain Hong Kong's export performance. On local factors, although stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, private consumption is expected to grow moderately, weighed down by rising interest rates. With increased housing supply and the commencement of several infrastructure projects, building and construction activities should grow steadily, but sluggish business sentiment and rising interest rates will suppress corporate capital expenditure. The Government currently forecasts real GDP growth of between 2% and 3% in 2017, while the average forecast of private-sector analysts is 2.0%. The outlook for economic growth is subject to numerous uncertainties, particularly those arising from the external environment. Policy uncertainty under the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, with the possible emergence of trade protectionist policies posing headwinds to global trade flows. The Brexit process and the general elections in several major European countries may also lead to asset market volatility and affect fund flows of the Hong Kong dollar. In addition, the normalisation of US interest rates will tighten local monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, although local inflation has gained momentum on a quarter-on-quarter basis in recent months, it has remained moderate overall. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index stabilised at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January this year (Chart 3.4). The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, then declined slightly to 2.4% in January. The rise in inflation momentum was mainly due to increases in prices of traded goods and housing rentals (Chart 3.5). In particular, inflation in the prices of traded goods rose from negative in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, mainly driven by prices of basic foodstuffs as well as clothing and footwear. At the same time, since the third quarter, as the decline in private residential rentals narrowed and public housing rentals were raised in September 2016, the housing rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index rose, but subsequently eased slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Various measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer price inflation by major component Chart 3.6 Composite Consumer Price Index rental component and market rentals In the near term, owing to weak import prices and moderate local cost pressures, inflationary pressure is expected to remain under control. As the strength of the Hong Kong dollar offsets to some extent the impact of the rebound in global commodity prices, imported inflation will remain low (Chart 3.7). On the local front, the output gap in the fourth quarter of 2016 is estimated to have remained close to zero, which should help ease business cost pressures and thus contain inflation in the services component. Despite the tight labour market, wage increases in recent quarters have been mild, with real wages per capita rising by 1.1% in the first half of 2016, then falling by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Given the persistent uncertainty in the external environment leading to cautious business sentiment, against this backdrop, the increase in labour costs should be restrained. In addition, owing to the weak retail sales performance in recent months, the increase in retail property rentals is expected to be moderate. Furthermore, the impact of the earlier softening in private residential rentals will gradually emerge, which will also help ease inflationary pressure. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate for the whole of 2017 is expected to decline, with the Government forecasting an underlying inflation rate of 2.0% for the year, lower than the 2.3% in 2016. Chart 3.7 Commodity and import prices Chart 3.8 Unit labour cost and real wages per capita The inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. On the downside, if inflation in the US accelerates under the Trump administration, this could lead to a faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes, which may push up local mortgage rates and increase downward pressure on property prices and housing rentals. At the same time, the appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar may keep import prices weak, while also weakening Hong Kong's appeal to visitors. On the upside, if the global economic expansion is faster than expected, it may accelerate Hong Kong's economic growth and push up demand-driven international commodity prices, thereby exerting upward pressure on local inflation. In addition, the revised statutory minimum wage will take effect on 1 May 2017, which may push inflation further upward, but the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed on to consumer prices.

Despite volatility in financial markets, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained largely stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates rose alongside US dollar interbank rates. Partly due to an improving local economic environment, overall loans continued to grow moderately. Looking ahead, amid a faster pace of US interest rate normalisation, an unclear policy direction of the new US administration, and political risks in Europe, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although the market volatility triggered by the November US presidential election led to a general depreciation of Asian currencies, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar held steady. However, the interest rate projections released by the US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on 13-14 December 2016 prompted heightened market expectations of a faster pace of US rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken briefly thereafter. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened somewhat in line with other Asian currencies, but as market expectations of a US rate hike in March rose from mid-February, the Hong Kong dollar began to show signs of weakening. During the reporting period, the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange rate and fund flow indicators; Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators. As the US dollar strengthened, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar rose by 4.9% between August and December, before stabilising more recently (Chart 4.3). As the impact of a narrowing inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was mild, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar closely tracked the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Portfolio investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest balance of payments statistics show that non-resident investment in equity and debt securities recorded net inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and substantial initial public offering activity (Table 4.A). However, driven partly by Hong Kong banks increasing their holdings of US bonds, residents' debt investment recorded sizeable outflows, outweighing the inflows of non-resident investment. As a result, cross-border portfolio investment recorded net outflows in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds showed portfolio investment outflows in the final quarter of 2016, mainly due to the unexpected US presidential election result, coupled with expectations of a faster pace of US rate hikes, which placed local financial markets and other Asian markets under pressure (Chart 4.4). However, the latest data show that Hong Kong portfolio investment experienced inflow pressure in the first quarter of 2017, partly because investors were optimistic about the US adopting an expansionary fiscal policy, improving the performance of global financial markets. Chart 4.4 Market surveys of equity- and bond-related fund flows. Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. A faster pace of US interest rate normalisation would heighten the risk of a reversal in Hong Kong dollar fund flows. At the same time, amid uncertainties over the new US administration, the Brexit process, and elections in EU member states, fund flows may become more volatile. In addition, increased investment demand from Mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may generate inflow pressure on the Hong Kong dollar. Although northbound trading exceeded southbound trading in size in the initial period following the launch of the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment fund flows between the Mainland and Hong Kong under the scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite rising US dollar interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained sizeable, rising a further 1.7% in the second half of the year, driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the sum of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly at a high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Among these, as an additional HK$49 billion of Exchange Fund Bills was issued to meet banks' strong demand for liquidity management, the Aggregate Balance contracted while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes rose correspondingly. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base. As the local economy became more robust, the pace of Hong Kong dollar money supply growth quickened. The growth of Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) accelerated from 2.3% in the first half of the year to 6.5% in the second half. As the major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits recorded faster growth of 6.6% in the second half of the year (Chart 4.7), mainly driven by stronger local economic activity and increased transactional demand from a pickup in initial public offering activity. In terms of counterpart assets analysis, the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 mainly reflected an increase in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks' net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), which reflected respectively the money created from credit expansion and the net inflow of Hong Kong dollar funds into the non-bank private sector. Chart 4.6 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterpart assets. On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits remained mixed. After growing 10.2% in the first half of the year, US dollar deposits recorded a higher increase of 12.8% in the second half amid US dollar strength (Chart 4.7). By contrast, other foreign currency deposits contracted a further 10.3%, mainly due to a decline in renminbi deposits. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions grew by 6.2% in the second half of 2016, with full-year growth of 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth. Amid expectations of US interest rate normalisation, banks' wholesale funding costs rose in the fourth quarter of 2016. While Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained low, they rose somewhat, driven partly by year-end funding demand and catching up with the increase in US dollar interbank interest rates. The overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose by 54 and 46 basis points respectively in the second half of the year to 0.66% and 1.02% (Chart 4.8). At the same time, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward in line with the US dollar yield curve, with the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rising by about 90 basis points to close at 1.93% at the end of December. Entering early 2017, as funding demand eased, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally declined, while yields on long-term Hong Kong Government Bonds also edged down along with US government bond yields. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates and 10-year government bond yields. Owing to the banking system's large deposit base, the rise in retail-level interest rates was relatively small. Banks' average funding cost (measured by the composite interest rate) remained low, rising only 6 basis points in January 2017 from seven months earlier to 0.32% (Chart 4.9). Owing to relatively stable funding costs and intensified competition in the mortgage lending business, the average interest rate on new mortgages fell to a recent low of 1.71% in October 2016, before rebounding to 2.07% in January 2017 in line with the rise in the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. Chart 4.9 Composite interest rate and average interest rate on new mortgages. Looking ahead, the pace of increase in local interest rates will depend on the speed of US interest rate normalisation, the scale of capital outflows, and global macro-financial developments. Upward pressure on local interest rates, coupled with a rise in the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate along with the US dollar exchange rate, may reduce the support provided by local financial conditions to the real economy. Box 4 discusses the compilation of a Hong Kong financial conditions index for monitoring local financial conditions. Owing to stronger local economic activity and rising cross-border funding demand, overall loans, after growing 2.2% in the first half of the year, rose a further 4.2% in the second half (Chart 4.10). As economic growth momentum picked up, local loan growth accelerated slightly from 3.2% in the first half of the year to 4.0% in the second half. Loans used outside Hong Kong, after edging down slightly in the first half of the year, rebounded 4.6% in the second half, partly reflecting rising year-end funding demand from multinational corporations. By currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half of the year, while foreign currency loans also recorded moderate growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually scaled back repayments of foreign currency loans. For 2016 as a whole, overall loans grew moderately by 6.5%, compared with 3.5% in 2015. Chart 4.10 Loan growth. By economic sector, local loans performed unevenly in the second half of the year (Chart 4.11). Loans to financial and finance-related enterprises and the information technology sector recorded double-digit growth in the second half of the year, reflecting to some extent the strong funding demand driven by better growth prospects in these sectors. Loans to the construction industry and property development also accelerated along with increased private construction activity. On the other hand, despite signs of improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, trade financing and loans to the manufacturing, wholesale and retail sectors declined. Chart 4.11 Local loan growth in individual sectors. Household debt growth accelerated to 4.3% in the second half of the year, compared with 0.5% in the first half. Within household debt, partly reflecting an improving economic environment, personal loans (including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes) rose 7.2% (Chart 4.11), and residential mortgage loan growth accelerated to 3.1%, mainly reflecting brisk residential transactions during July to October. As a result, the ratio of household debt to GDP also rose from 65.8% in the second quarter of 2016 to 67.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 The ratio of household debt to GDP and its components. Banks' funding positions remained broadly stable. Reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down from 78.2% at the end of June 2016 to 77.1% at the end of the year (Chart 4.13); at the same time, the overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell from 61.4% to 59.9% at the end of the year, with the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio dropping sharply to 63.8% due to strong growth in US dollar deposits. Chart 4.13 Loan-to-deposit ratios. Owing to expectations of rising interest rates and rapid changes in the macro-financial environment, there will be uncertainty over credit growth for some time to come. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook showed that loan demand remained soft in the near term. As the US dollar appreciated, both the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened (Chart 4.14). The offshore renminbi exchange rate was at a discount to the onshore renminbi exchange rate for most of the latter part of 2016, closing at its lowest level of the year of 6.98 against the US dollar at the end of 2016. The offshore renminbi interbank market again came under pressure from tightening liquidity in December, partly reflecting deteriorating financial market conditions and banks' precautionary funding demand before the year-end (Chart 4.15). As banks increased their liquidity buffers amid deteriorating market sentiment, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate once climbed to 61.3% on 6 January 2017. The rise in offshore renminbi funding costs subsequently led to the unwinding of offshore renminbi short positions, driving the offshore renminbi exchange rate to rebound in early January 2017, with offshore renminbi also turning to a premium over onshore renminbi. Since mid-January, both the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates have stabilised somewhat, liquidity conditions have gradually improved, and the overnight and three-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates fell to 2.00% and 4.61% respectively at the end of February 2017.

In the second half of 2016, the profitability of retail banks improved compared with the same period in 2015, owing to growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a reduction in loan impairment provisions. The banks' capital positions and asset quality also remained sound. Although the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) rose markedly following the US interest rate hike in December, the liquidity conditions of the banking sector remained favourable. The funding costs of retail banks stayed stable and at low levels, supported by a large retail deposit base. Nevertheless, banks should carefully assess the impact of a possibly faster-than-expected pace of US rate hikes, particularly the risk of substantial capital outflows and the subsequent potential effect on local interest rates. In addition, given the continued rise in leverage levels of non-local corporates, a substantial increase in interest rates could lead to a deterioration in the banks' asset quality. To strengthen the resilience of Hong Kong banks against systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio requirement will be raised to 1.875% with effect from 1 January 2018. The profitability of retail banks improved, with the return on assets rising from 0.95% in the second half of 2015 to 1.12% in the second half of 2016 (the red line in Chart 5.1). The improvement in profitability was driven by growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a reduction in loan impairment provisions. For the whole of 2016, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 8.7%, while the return on assets increased from 1.05% for the whole of 2015 to 1.10%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks. The net interest margin of retail banks continued to improve, reaching 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks. Wholesale funding costs in Hong Kong rose markedly after the US resumed rate hikes in December 2016. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR rose significantly by 33 basis points in December 2016, though it remained low by historical standards (the blue line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates. Nevertheless, the overall impact of the US rate hike on retail banks' Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained modest. As the main funding source of retail banks is retail deposits, and retail deposit rates remained stable and at low levels even after the rate hike, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds of retail banks, edged up by only 5 basis points to 0.31% in December 2016 after remaining at a low level of around 0.26% for more than a year. On a broader level, a similar picture emerged for the total Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. Although the average Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of banks in the non-deposit market rose by 28 basis points in the second half of 2016, the increase in the average deposit funding cost in the retail market was smaller, rising by only 11 basis points. Overall, the average total Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks rose by 17 basis points (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturity of licensed banks. The extent and pace of the rise in HIBOR both exceeded those of Hong Kong banks' funding costs, which may benefit some retail banks. This is because they have actively promoted HIBOR-based mortgage loans over the past few years, and the rise in interest rates on such loans may help widen their overall net interest margin. However, the improvement in net interest margin may be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In fact, there are signs that some banks have lowered the spread between their mortgage rates and the benchmark and/or offered more attractive mortgage terms to attract customers. In the long run, as the US will raise interest rates further, banks may soon face pressure from rising retail deposit rates, thereby affecting their funding costs and having a more significant impact on their net interest margins. The banks' capital levels remained strong and well above international minimum requirements. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a high level of 19.2% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital adequacy ratio was 16.4%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capital levels of locally incorporated authorized institutions. 1. Consolidated position. 2. Locally incorporated authorized institutions are required to comply with the revised capital adequacy framework, Basel III, which took effect on 1 January 2013. Therefore, the capital adequacy ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with the data up to December 2012. Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained favourable during the reporting period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of Category 1 institutions, although edging down from 158.0% in the second quarter of 2016 to 156.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016, remained at a high level (Chart 5.6). The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions also remained stable at 51.0%. Both ratios remained well above their respective minimum regulatory requirements, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector is able to withstand liquidity shocks arising from possible capital outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.6 Liquidity Coverage Ratio. Customer deposits remained the main funding source of retail banks. The proportion of customer deposits in the banks' total liabilities rose from 71.7% at the end of June 2016 to 73.1% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.7). Chart 5.7 Liability structure of retail banks. As the total loans and advances and total deposits of retail banks grew at similar rates during the reporting period, the loan-to-deposit ratio in all currencies remained stable at 57.0% in December 2016 (Chart 5.8). During the same period, the loan-to-deposit ratios in Hong Kong dollars and foreign currencies also remained broadly unchanged. Chart 5.8 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of retail banks. Although the interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks rose slightly, it remained at a low level. Estimates show that, under a hypothetical across-the-board interest rate shock of 200 basis points, the possible decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 3.92% of their total capital base as at December 2016 (Chart 5.9). Nevertheless, given that the pace of US interest rate normalisation may be faster than expected following the US presidential election, banks should assess the impact of this situation on their interest rate risk management. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the impact on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of the banks' total capital base. During the reporting period, the asset quality of retail banks' loan portfolios remained sound. At the end of December 2016, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio remained at low levels of 0.72% and 0.53% respectively. Both ratios remained low by historical standards (Chart 5.10). Chart 5.10 Asset quality of retail banks. Although asset quality currently remains sound by historical standards, banks in Hong Kong should continue to pay attention to the external environment; as the assessment in Box 5 shows, loans used outside Hong Kong by the banking sector have recorded rapid growth since the global financial crisis, reflecting that the banks' asset quality would be more susceptible to the external environment. Banks' expectations of short-term credit growth were mixed. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2016 showed that, although most of the surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, the proportion of surveyed authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months edged up to 14% (Table 5.A). In the second half of 2016, the credit risk of unsecured personal loans remained manageable, with the annualised credit card charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio falling to 1.92% and 0.24% respectively at the end of December (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio of credit card lending and bankruptcy petition cases. The banks' mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying at 0.03% at the end of December. The average loan-to-value ratio of newly approved mortgages was 51.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.12). This loan-to-value ratio was well below the 64% recorded in September 2009, before the HKMA began implementing seven rounds of countercyclical macroprudential measures. However, the debt servicing index of new mortgages⁴⁷ rose from 44.0 in the second quarter of 2016 to 48.8 in the fourth quarter (the red line in Chart 5.12), mainly reflecting the rise in the average amount of new mortgage loans (Chart 5.13). The continued pursuit of interest rate normalisation by the US may further increase personal debt burdens. A sensitivity test showed that, if interest rates rose by 300 basis points with other conditions unchanged, the index could rise significantly to 67.3 within four quarters.⁴⁸ Banks should remain vigilant about the risk of a continued rise in personal debt burdens. Chart 5.12 Average loan-to-value ratio of new mortgage loans and personal debt burden. Chart 5.13 New mortgage loans of surveyed authorized institutions. The pace of US rate hikes remains the main factor affecting the credit risk of corporate loans. However, the extent to which the asset quality of individual banks is actually affected depends on the characteristics of their corporate loan portfolios. In particular, based on our assessment using accounting data of non-financial companies listed in Hong Kong, we found that the leverage ratio trends of local and non-local corporates diverged significantly after the global financial crisis, with non-local corporates being more susceptible to debt servicing problems.⁵⁰ Banks should assess the impact of rate hikes on the credit risk of loans to non-local corporates. Specifically, corporate leverage, as measured by the weighted average debt-to-equity ratio, rose after the global financial crisis, with the increase driven mainly by non-local corporates. The leverage ratio of non-local corporates rose to 85% in the first half of 2016 (the red line in Chart 5.14), while the leverage ratio of local corporates remained broadly stable.
