Global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year as markets reassessed inflation risks in the United States. In February, global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, completely offsetting the notable gains recorded at the start of the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The sustained rise in global equity markets over the past two years amid low volatility was underpinned by market expectations of an ideal scenario in which the economic environment would continue to grow steadily while inflation and interest rates remained low. However, this expectation is now confronting risks arising from tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionist sentiment, and heightened geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, and markets continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, overall lending continued to increase, albeit at a more moderate pace. Following a slight moderation in the middle of last year, both the rate of increase in property prices and transaction volumes rebounded in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, the renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may add to the volatility of fund flows in Hong Kong. Given the uncertainties in financial markets, as well as the ongoing normalisation of US monetary policy and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant to the risks of increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels and the elevated level of household debt burden, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality should interest rates rise more than expected. After the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) had hovered at low levels for more than two years, global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. Global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, with the S&P 500 Index at one point declining by more than 10%, completely offsetting the notable gains recorded in early January. The shift in market sentiment stemmed from signs that the global economic recovery could exert pressure on long-subdued US wages and prices, which could in turn prompt the Federal Reserve to accelerate the pace of its interest rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rise in global equity markets over the past two years was built on market expectations that economic conditions would remain favourable. In the second half of 2017, global economic growth momentum continued to strengthen, with economic activity in advanced and emerging market economies picking up in tandem. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform package that included tax cuts and comprehensive reforms of corporate and personal tax provisions, giving rise to market expectations that the strong US economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite the pick-up in activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained mild, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates would remain low over the long term. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rose significantly in 2017, with US equity markets in particular repeatedly setting new highs. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth data for January, global equity markets reassessed inflation risks. After the short-term volatility in financial markets, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the United States, the economy has now reached its output potential, and the cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from the anticipated tax cuts could accelerate a rebound in inflation, thereby prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. At the same time, as tax cuts will lead to a rising fiscal deficit, the United States may issue more Treasury bonds in the future, which is expected to add to the upward pressure on long-term bond yields while the Federal Reserve continues to advance the normalisation of its balance sheet. Outside the United States, the strengthening growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led markets to expect that their central banks may scale back their quantitative easing programmes. If implemented, this would result in a synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also cast a shadow over the global economic growth outlook. The US government appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel, and aluminium. These moves have raised concerns over whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. In addition, should geopolitical tensions escalate unexpectedly, this could affect global trade and exacerbate volatility in global financial markets. Given the aforementioned uncertainties surrounding the global economic outlook, it is questionable whether the currently elevated valuations of global asset markets can be sustained. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical increase in global demand and the rising fiscal deficit resulting from anticipated US tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R*); in addition, the Federal Reserve's balance sheet normalisation is expected to lead to a rise in the term premium, which could push up long-term interest rates and thereby weigh on asset market valuations. In East Asia, economies in the region were also in an ideal environment of steady growth and mild inflation. Alongside strong economic performance and an optimistic outlook, capital inflows also accelerated, and financial markets rose concurrently. However, this favourable outlook faces downside risks from a range of factors: the tightening of global liquidity resulting from major central banks synchronously advancing monetary policy normalisation; the US government's pursuit of inward-looking trade policies; heightened geopolitical tensions; and the possibility that offshore US dollar liquidity may tighten as US corporations repatriate profits to the United States on a large scale in response to the one-off "deemed repatriation" provision under the country's tax reform. Should credit and financial markets face any shocks, this could trigger a reversal of capital flows, with more highly leveraged sectors and economies being the most vulnerable to the impact of tightening financial conditions. On the Mainland of China, supported by factors such as steady consumption, robust infrastructure, and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year, the Mainland economy performed well in the second half of 2017. At the same time, signs of the rise of the "new economy" became increasingly evident, with high value-added sectors such as manufacturing and services demonstrating strong business expansion momentum over the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term economic growth outlook remains positive, though uncertainties persist. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term pressure on growth arising from the further advancement of structural reforms. The Mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would continue to adopt a proactive fiscal policy stance, which may help ease adverse economic developments where necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in both structural reforms and the control of systemic risks. In particular, following the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland property market showed signs of cooling during the review period, especially in first-tier cities. At the same time, as banks tightened their loan approval standards, banks' risk exposure to corporates in industries with excess capacity remained under control, while shadow banking activities also slowed amid financial deleveraging. In addition to the above positive developments, our analysis also indicates that the efficiency of capital allocation on the Mainland appears to have improved. In particular, the borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capacity appear to have tightened, possibly due to a reduction in support provided by local governments (for details, please refer to Box 2 on page 28). On the external front, amid a more stable economic situation and diminishing risks, capital outflow pressures remained mild for most of 2017. The Hong Kong economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP grew by 3.8% for the whole of 2017, the fastest pace in nearly six years. Owing to favourable employment and income conditions as well as rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2017. Overall investment expenditure also rebounded on the back of increased corporate capital expenditure. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further. Nonetheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services contributed positively to GDP growth. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. Private consumption, building and construction activities, and exports will continue to support economic growth. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. The Government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2018 are in the range of 3 to 4% and 3.0% respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned above, the Mainland's economic performance amid tightening financial conditions, and the trend of Hong Kong's asset markets. Although the unemployment rate fell to 2.9%, a near-20-year low, local inflationary pressures remained under control. However, there were signs that quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum edged up slightly in recent months, with the prices of both tradable goods and services rising. Looking ahead, the underlying inflation rate may edge up to a still-moderate level, partly reflecting the pass-through effect of rising rents on newly signed private residential leases. Affected by funding demand from new share issuance/fundraising activities and seasonal funding demand, liquidity conditions tightened, and the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions increased, prompting the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate to strengthen between September and November 2017. As liquidity conditions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities became active again, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened again from December 2017. In early 2018, despite the turbulence in global financial markets (particularly in equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened further in early March 2018, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates were under upward pressure between September and December 2017. This was mainly attributable to funding demand from new share issuance/fundraising activities and banks' prudent approach to liquidity management towards the end of the year. In December, the average overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively from six months earlier, to 0.25% and 1.26%. After edging down slightly in early January 2018, HIBOR remained broadly stable and was not affected by the recent adjustment in global financial markets. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, the average interest rate on banks' new mortgages still followed the upward trend of short-term HIBOR, rising to 2.16% in December. On the other hand, retail banks' funding costs generally remained low after a brief rise in October due to new share issuance/fundraising activities, with the composite interest rate closing at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure; and if global financial market sentiment shifts sharply, the volatility of fund flows may increase. For the whole of 2017, total bank lending grew steadily by 16.1%. Following strong growth of 10.2% in the first half, loan growth slowed to 5.3% in the second half. Among these, the growth rate of both domestic loans and loans used outside Hong Kong declined across most sectors. Foreign currency loan growth slowed, partly due to rising US dollar funding costs. Meanwhile, owing to the favourable local economic environment and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to record rapid growth. As Hong Kong dollar loans grew faster than deposits, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose in the second half of 2017, climbing to 82.7% at year-end, a high since March 2015. On the other hand, owing to the relatively slow growth of foreign currency loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 63.1% at year-end. The onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilising between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened significantly against most major currencies, the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened somewhat from December. Following a slight decline in the first half, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool (comprising total renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit) rebounded slightly in the second half, broadly reflecting changes in market expectations regarding the renminbi exchange rate. As for other offshore renminbi business, although renminbi loans continued to decline, the amount of renminbi trade settlement handled by Hong Kong banks rebounded in the second half. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the advancement of the "Belt and Road" Initiative and the continued internationalisation of the renminbi.

The synchronised strengthening of the global economy since late 2016 has shown no signs of abating. Improved growth prospects drove global equity markets higher throughout 2017 and into early 2018. However, as markets reassessed US inflation risks, global equity markets experienced a sell-off and sharp volatility in February, marking the end of the calm that had prevailed in financial markets over the preceding two years. Looking ahead, the risk of tightening global financial conditions, along with a range of policy and event risks, will continue to cast a shadow over the global outlook. Against the backdrop of a tight labour market, US tax cuts could accelerate a cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to quicken the pace of monetary policy tightening. As the Federal Reserve continues to advance balance sheet normalisation, increased US Treasury issuance to fund tax cuts may add upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The looming threat of rising trade barriers, together with any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions, could also pose a threat to the nascent recovery in global trade. In East Asia, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017, buoyed by strong export performance and stable domestic demand. Nevertheless, while the economic outlook is optimistic, it is also subject to various downside risks, such as global monetary conditions tightening more than expected, US inward-looking trade policies and geopolitical tensions. Should these downside risks materialise, they would also increase the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers face multiple challenges: on the one hand, they must guard against the risks to economic growth, while on the other, they must limit the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, economic performance was strong in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and in containing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties persist, and this will partly depend on the extent to which the rapid growth of the "new economy" can offset the short-term pressure on growth arising from the further advancement of structural reforms. As economic conditions stabilised and risks diminished, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. As the momentum of cyclical economic improvement has grown increasingly firm since late 2016, growth in advanced and emerging market economies accelerated in tandem in 2017. Among the major advanced economies, the US saw robust growth in investment and exports, driven by upbeat private-sector sentiment and a substantial depreciation of the US dollar, while the euro area and Japan also recorded broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports of emerging market economies also benefited from the stabilisation of global commodity prices and increased import demand from major advanced economies. In the near term, following the passage of US tax reform, investment and consumption are expected to receive a further boost from reductions in corporate and personal income taxes. In view of the current cyclical economic upswing and the expansionary effects of US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund forecast in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real gross domestic product growth forecasts As growth momentum in the euro area and Japan strengthened, markets expected the divergence in global monetary policy to narrow, which, together with a more optimistic global growth outlook, stimulated risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby putting pressure on the US dollar. Although the Federal Reserve raised interest rates three times during the year and began to advance balance sheet normalisation, the US dollar index still recorded a decline of nearly 10% in 2017. At the same time, despite the broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in major advanced economies remained subdued and below their central banks' targets, leading markets until recently to expect global interest rates to remain low (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global equity markets continued to rise throughout 2017 and into early 2018, with the S&P 500 index repeatedly hitting record highs, pushing the cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratio up to 33.8 in January 2018, its highest level since the "dot-com bubble" in early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core inflation in major advanced economies However, since the second half of 2017, market concerns that tax cuts would lead to rising fiscal deficits and inflation have driven US long-term Treasury yields steadily higher, calling into question the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset market valuations. As the US reported a higher-than-expected increase in average hourly wages for January 2018, markets reassessed US inflation risks, triggering a correction in global equity markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 index at one point fell by more than 10% from its high on 26 January, completely offsetting the significant gains made at the start of the year, and continued to come under pressure after the US government announced a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged sharply, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index spiking to a two-year high of 37.3 at one point, marking the end of the sustained low-volatility environment of the preceding two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, following the short-term equity market volatility, US inflation risks, the risk of rising US long-term bond yields, and the possibility of other major central banks tightening monetary policy could all lead to a tightening of global monetary conditions, thereby casting a shadow over the global economic outlook. First, with regard to US inflation risks, the recently passed tax reform includes several provisions expected to provide short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The main measures involved in the tax reform include: (1) lowering corporate and personal income tax rates; (2) temporarily allowing full expensing of capital investment; and (3) a one-off "deemed repatriation" provision that helps reduce the incentive for US firms to park their overseas earnings abroad. While it remains uncertain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, as the US economy has now reached its output potential, the tax cuts could push US output above its potential level, leading to overheating and a cyclical rebound in inflation. Should inflationary pressures rise more than expected, this could prompt the Federal Reserve to quicken the pace of monetary policy tightening. At present, the path of the federal funds rate expected by financial markets is flatter than the projections published by the Federal Reserve. However, should inflation rebound unexpectedly, the risk of a sudden repricing of interest rate expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Federal funds rate projections Second, given that the tax reform could exacerbate the fiscal deficit, US Treasury issuance is expected to increase going forward. As the Federal Reserve continues to implement its balance sheet normalisation plan, this is expected to lead to a rise in the term premium; in this context, increased US Treasury issuance may intensify the upward pressure on long-term bond yields. Moreover, as markets increasingly anticipated the likelihood of the US passing the tax cut plan, US inflation expectations have risen steadily since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). Consequently, after hovering at low levels for most of 2017, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield has risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns over increased Treasury supply pressures and rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.5 Five-year, five-year forward inflation expectations In addition, a key question is whether the natural rate of interest (R*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain low over the long term as most expect. Although estimates of R* vary, it is generally agreed that it has fallen substantially since the global financial crisis (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, US R* may face upside risks in the future, owing to (1) an expected decline in the national savings rate resulting from increased fiscal deficits, and (2) a possible rise in the investment rate driven by corporate tax cuts and more favourable tax treatment of capital expenditure. A rise in R*, together with the expected increase in the term premium arising from the Federal Reserve's balance sheet normalisation, could signal higher long-term interest rates, thereby weighing on asset market valuations. Chart 2.6 US R* estimated using the Laubach-Williams model Third, the strengthening growth momentum in the euro area and Japan has led markets to expect that their central banks may scale back monetary easing. Should this occur, it could signal a synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. In the euro area, member economies recorded broad-based cyclical expansion (Chart 2.7). As for Japan, its economic recovery has also accelerated, with real gross domestic product recording its eighth consecutive quarter of positive growth in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan have continued to signal the maintenance of accommodative monetary policy amid subdued inflation, the clearer growth outlook for the euro area and Japan (and the continued tightening of Japan's labour market) has led some market participants to predict that they will further scale back their quantitative easing programmes in the near future. Chart 2.7 Real gross domestic product of selected euro area member states Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also pose a threat to the nascent global economic growth and trade recovery. The US government appears more inclined to adopt inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries, recent examples being the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines in January 2018 and the announcement of import tariffs on steel and aluminium in early March, raising concerns over whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. At the same time, the UK and the rest of the EU are currently negotiating post-Brexit trade arrangements, a process fraught with numerous uncertainties. Should these developments lead to increased trade frictions, they could hamper global trade flows and reduce global production efficiency. Moreover, an unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions (such as military conflict on the Korean peninsula, political turmoil in the Middle East and the latent risk of terrorist attacks) could increase volatility in global financial markets. In East Asia, economic growth momentum strengthened further in the second half of 2017, ending the year on a strong note. Real growth in 2017 accelerated to 4.3%, the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained the main driver of growth, while domestic demand also provided steady support (Chart 2.8). The accelerating recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in Mainland China, and a rebound in global demand for technology products all boosted the region's exports. Chart 2.8 East Asia: domestic demand and exports Inflationary pressures have remained subdued to date. In the second half of 2017, headline inflation in East Asia eased, affected by lower food price inflation and stable energy prices (Chart 2.9). At the same time, owing to slow wage growth in several economies, core consumer price inflation (excluding food and energy) remained at relatively low levels. Chart 2.9 East Asia: headline and core consumer price inflation rate* Note: Since 2016, South Korea has set its inflation target at 2%, with a band of +/-0.5%. Sources: CEIC and central banks. The improving economy, accompanied by substantial capital inflows, drove financial asset prices significantly higher in 2017 and early 2018 (Chart 2.10, blue and pink bars). Capital inflows into the region's markets rebounded significantly in 2017, with total portfolio investment inflows reaching a high not seen since 2010. Valuations of various financial assets in the region also rose along with the markets. Indeed, credit risk premia in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, while benchmark equity indices across the region all rose. Regional currencies generally appreciated against the US dollar.

Amid buoyant local demand and improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained solid growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth in 2018 is expected to remain robust. The outlook for the Hong Kong economy remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalisation of monetary policy by major central banks, concerns over the stability of global financial markets, rising protectionist sentiment, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions. In the near term, although local inflationary pressures should remain mild, certain upside risks persist. The Hong Kong economy sustained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real Gross Domestic Product grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, similar to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow robustly and remained one of the key drivers of GDP growth. The solid consumption growth was attributable to favourable employment and income conditions, still-optimistic consumer sentiment, and the positive impact of rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although building and construction activities weakened, increased corporate capital expenditure led overall investment spending to rise notably in the final quarter, after remaining broadly stable for three quarters. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components; Chart 3.2 Real Imports and Exports. The sustained economic growth momentum drove an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. During the period, total employment rose by about 0.7% to over 3.85 million persons, with the most notable increases in the construction sector, the financing and business services sector, and the public administration, social and personal services sector. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, labour productivity showed further signs of improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from an improving global economic growth outlook and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. On the local front, private consumption is expected to continue growing, mainly due to favourable labour market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. As for local fixed capital formation, benefiting from increased housing supply and the continued rollout of infrastructure projects, building and construction activities should grow steadily. Although an improving economic environment will stimulate business capital expenditure, potential increases in interest rates could have a negative impact. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 3 to 4% in 2018, while growth forecasts by international institutions and private-sector analysts range from 2 to 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in previous sections, the economic performance of Mainland China amid tightening financial conditions, and the movements of Hong Kong's asset markets. Local inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, but sequential inflation momentum has shown signs of a slight pickup in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, similar to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the underlying inflation rate on a three-month-on-three-month annualised basis, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Both traded goods and services prices rose. The pickup in newly signed private residential rentals since mid-2016 may also have added to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressures in recent quarters continued to remain mild (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Various Indicators of Consumer Price Inflation; Chart 3.4 Rental Component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and Market Rentals; Chart 3.5 Unit Labour Cost and Per Capita Wages. As global inflation remains mild and local cost increases are stable, Hong Kong's inflationary pressures are expected to remain mild in 2018, but the underlying inflation rate may gradually rise from its eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For example, owing to the pass-through effect of growth in newly signed private residential rentals, inflationary pressures may increase somewhat in the second half of 2018. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation at a moderate 2.2% in 2018, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is mild, upside risks persist. On the external front, should global inflation or commodity prices record larger-than-expected increases, this could add to local inflation momentum. On the local front, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, dropping below 3% for the first time in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero, and a significant tightening of the labour market could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment Rate. Amid low interest rates following the global financial crisis in 2008, the mortgage debt of Hong Kong households increased. As the normalisation of US dollar interest rates progresses, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually follow US dollar interest rates upward, and household mortgage repayment burdens will increase accordingly in the future, thereby weighing on household consumption. This Box therefore examines the impact of an increased mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage repayment burden refers to the ratio of mortgage debt-servicing payments (i.e., interest payments plus the amortisation of loan principal) to income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage repayment burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, and the wealth and collateral effects arising from changes in asset prices as mentioned in general economic theory, in the presence of a mortgage repayment burden, interest rate shocks also affect private consumption by altering mortgage interest payments and, in turn, households' disposable income. This impact will be amplified as the amount of outstanding mortgage loans increases. Furthermore, the amount of loan principal amortisation varies with changes in the amount of outstanding mortgage loans, which also affects private consumption by altering households' disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of Private Consumption. To measure the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption, we estimated the Outstanding Mortgage Debt-Servicing Ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike current mortgage repayment burden indicators that apply only to newly originated mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debt of overall households, which is more closely related to total private consumption. Broadly following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measured the OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed instalment payments: where Dt is the amount of outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt is the total income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st are respectively the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage repayment burden of the entire household sector, it is useful to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used repayment burden indicators. Chart B3.2 shows the OMDSR estimates from 1985 to mid-2017, as well as the median mortgage payment and loan repayment to income ratios estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial population census. In the early 2000s, both ratios exhibited a downward trend, consistent with the reduction in overall household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the 1997 property bubble and the sharp decline in mortgage interest rates over the same period. Despite the substantial rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable, owing to the macroprudential measures taken by the HKMA on bank mortgage lending, which curbed overall household mortgage leverage. In addition, the lengthening of the maturity of newly originated mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage payments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and the Median Mortgage Payment and Loan Repayment to Income Ratios. We also compared the OMDSR with banks' debt-servicing ratio, the latter being the actual debt-servicing to income ratio of banks' new mortgage applicants. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks' debt-servicing ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. As existing mortgages were originated when property prices were lower, their repayments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, the outstanding mortgage repayment burden indicator covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e., the OMDSR) is lower than the repayment burden indicator for new mortgages (i.e., banks' debt-servicing ratio). Moreover, banks' debt-servicing ratio is higher also because banks, in compliance with the HKMA's prudential supervisory requirements, take non-mortgage loan repayments into account when calculating the debt-servicing ratio. After the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks' debt-servicing ratio remained stable, mainly owing to the prudential supervision of mortgage lending implemented by the HKMA, which set a cap on banks' debt-servicing ratio, and this measure also helped to stabilise the OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and Banks' Debt-Servicing Ratio for New Mortgages. Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with the commonly used repayment burden indicators, but the OMDSR has greater timeliness and can reflect the burden of overall outstanding mortgage debt, rather than only that of newly originated mortgage debt. Therefore, we believe that using the OMDSR can assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimated an error-correction model following the methodology of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (proxied by real average private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented in the short-run equation by an error-correction term. Based on existing theory and empirical evidence, we adopt real income (proxied by median household income, deflated by the Composite Consumer Price Index), real housing and financial wealth (proxied by residential prices and the Hang Seng Index respectively, deflated by the Composite Consumer Price Index), and the OMDSR as the long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, while the local interbank market continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, but the pace of growth slowed compared with the first half. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Should sentiment in global financial markets shift abruptly, the volatility of fund flows may increase. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar traded between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate strengthened briefly during September to November 2017 and remained near the 7.80 level. This was mainly due to increased funding demand from new share fund-raising activities and banks' cautious approach to liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end, which led to tighter liquidity conditions, in turn slowing interest rate arbitrage activities and increasing the unwinding of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar. As the tightness in Hong Kong dollar liquidity eased and commercial demand for US dollars rose towards year-end, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets (especially equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar continued to function in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar softened, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators. The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly in line with the movement of the US dollar against most major currencies. As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar continued to closely track the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Portfolio investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that equity securities investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting an improving regional economic outlook and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Debt securities investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting the outflows of debt investment by residents. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that, amid optimism about the economic outlook and corporate earnings, both equity and debt investment recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017. In recent weeks, the survey data indicated that despite corrections in global financial markets, equity investment still recorded inflows, while bond investment recorded slight outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy normalisation process continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, which may lead to increased arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility that the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking of the Hong Kong dollar will be triggered cannot be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. At the same time, given that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation remains uncertain, and that global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment are changing rapidly, the volatility of Hong Kong dollar fund flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to make every effort to safeguard the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board mechanism. Although the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates and continued to shrink its balance sheet, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and recently. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base rose further by 1.4%, mainly driven by the growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued to back the issuance of banknotes (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the total of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained largely unchanged in the second half, staying at around HK$1,226.8 billion. Of this, the Aggregate Balance contracted, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills (totalling HK$80 billion) to meet banks' strong demand for liquidity management. Entering 2018, despite the stock market correction, the monetary base remained stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the monetary base. Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar money supply grew further in the second half of 2017, but at a slower pace. The growth of Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose slightly by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Of this, demand deposits grew faster in the second half, partly because of buoyant asset markets and rising investment demand. Analysis of the counterpart assets showed that the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 was, on the one hand, supported by the strong growth of Hong Kong dollar loans (Chart 4.6), and on the other hand, dragged down by net outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector and the contraction of banks' net foreign currency assets. Chart 4.6 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterpart assets. On the other hand, foreign currency deposit growth was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, the growth rate of US dollar deposits fell from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). By contrast, other foreign currency deposits, after declining for over two years, rebounded significantly in the second half, rising by 8.4%. This was mainly driven by the recent rebound in renminbi deposits. As the growth of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits slowed, total deposits with authorized institutions rose slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with a growth of 5.6% in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth. During September to December 2017, funding demand from new share fund-raising activities rose, and banks adopted a cautious approach to liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end, which put upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, the overnight and 3-month HIBOR rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, climbing in December to 0.25% and 1.26% respectively (on a monthly average basis). The negative interest rate differential between the 1-month to 3-month Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank rates also narrowed accordingly. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates. Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward but flattened, broadly in line with the movement of the US dollar yield curve. In the second half, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government bonds rose by 63 basis points, closing at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government bonds rose by a smaller 33 basis points, closing at 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average interest rate on new mortgage loans. Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to function in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand subsided, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates eased in early January. Thereafter, despite corrections in global and local stock markets, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates remained largely stable. The overnight and 3-month HIBOR closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. At the retail level, although banks' lending rates rose along with the surge in HIBOR, banks' funding costs generally remained low owing to the still-large deposit base. Despite keen competition in the mortgage business, banks' average interest rate on new mortgage loans gradually rose by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly following the upward movement of the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the composite interest rate, which measures the Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, although it rose briefly in October owing to increased funding demand from new share fund-raising activities, remained soft for most of the second half, closing at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, and as other major economies may begin interest rate normalisation, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, fluctuating global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase the volatility of fund flows. Nevertheless, the large Hong Kong dollar monetary base can act as a buffer, helping to moderate any excessively rapid rise in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. In addition, banks' prudent liquidity management and access to the Discount Window also help contain excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. The loan growth rate reached 10.2% in the first half and slowed to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). In the second half of 2017, the growth of both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed. Analysed by currency, owing to the favourable local economic environment and the relatively low funding cost of the Hong Kong dollar, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, while foreign currency loans rose only slightly by 0.1%. Of this, the growth of US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly because of rising US dollar funding costs. For 2017 as a whole, total loans recorded strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan growth. The growth of loans for use in Hong Kong (including trade finance) fell from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performances across the major sectors (Chart 4.11). The growth of loans to the building and construction and property development and investment sectors slowed in the second half, partly because, since June 2017, the authorities had required banks to strengthen risk management for lending to property developers. Although merchandise trade and retail sales further improved, loans for trade finance and to the transport sector recorded only relatively slight increases, while loans to the wholesale and retail sector recorded a decline. By contrast, the growth of loans to financial and financially-related enterprises remained strong, reflecting to some extent the steady expansion of the financial services industry. Chart 4.11 Growth of loans for use in Hong Kong by selected sectors. Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, personal loans (including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes) grew at a faster pace, rising by 12.4% in the second half. The strong growth of personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing from private banking and wealth management clients collateralised by financial assets. The growth of such loans was broadly similar to the continued growth in client assets managed by banks. The risk of such collateralised loans is manageable. In addition, the HKMA issued guidance to banks on the risk management of personal loans in January 2014, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting caps on loan tenors and borrowers' debt servicing ratios. On the other hand, although the volume of residential property transactions increased, the loan-to-value ratio of newly approved mortgages fell, and the growth of residential mortgage loans edged down slightly to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the ratio of household debt to GDP rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Benefiting mainly from the growth in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016. Their capital and liquidity positions remained sound. Following strong credit growth in the first half of 2017, credit growth moderated in the second half, while asset quality remained robust by historical standards. Despite a notable rise in the Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates, the Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks remained low due to low retail deposit rates. Nevertheless, banks should stay alert to the risks of increased interest rate volatility and possible fund outflows amid the normalisation of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the persistent rise in corporate leverage and the elevated level of personal debt burden, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality should interest rates rise more than expected. To strengthen banks' resilience against systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio in Hong Kong will be raised to 2.5% with effect from 1 January 2019.  In the second half of 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 13.6% compared with the same period a year earlier. This was mainly attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income and a reduction in loan impairment provisions, which together were sufficient to offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, the return on assets of retail banks edged down slightly from 1.17% in the first half to 1.15% in the second half of 2017. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 was still higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.1). For 2017 as a whole, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while the return on assets rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%.  Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks  The net interest margin of retail banks widened further from 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 (Chart 5.2). Observational evidence indicates that the improvement in net interest margin was consistent with the rise in the average spread of Hong Kong dollar corporate loans in the Hong Kong syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3).  Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Chart 5.3 Average spread of Hong Kong dollar syndicated loans  Since September 2017, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) have risen across the board, mainly driven by liquidity demand relating to initial public offerings and banks' liquidity needs towards the year-end, as well as by expectations of US interest rate hikes. In particular, the three-month HIBOR reached a post-financial-crisis high of 1.31% at the end of December 2017, up by 53 basis points from the end of June, though still at a relatively low level by historical standards (the blue line in Chart 5.4). Entering 2018, the HIBOR appeared to have stabilised as banks' year-end liquidity needs eased.  Despite the recent rise in HIBOR, the Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks remained stable. This was mainly due to low retail deposit rates during the review period. Against this backdrop, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds of retail banks, stayed at a low level of around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, and only edged up slightly to 0.38% at the end of December (the green line in Chart 5.4). A similar situation was observed in the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, the average Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of banks in the non-deposit market rose by 35 basis points, while the average deposit funding costs edged up slightly by 12 basis points. Overall, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks rose by 22 basis points (the red line in Chart 5.5).  Chart 5.4 Interest rates Chart 5.5 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks  The increase in HIBOR exceeded that of the overall funding costs of the Hong Kong banking sector, which may help improve the spreads on banks' assets benchmarked against HIBOR. However, this improvement may be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market data indicate that some banks have lowered the spread between their mortgage rates and the benchmark rate, or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms, in order to attract new customers. Given the expectation of further US interest rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater pressure from rising funding costs. In view of the intense competition in the loan market, if the increased funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers, this could put pressure on banks' net interest margins.  The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained well above the international minimum standards, indicating that the capital of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong. At the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased to 19.1% from 18.7% at the end of June (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio54 also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital.55  Chart 5.6 Capital position of locally incorporated authorized institutions  The HKMA recently issued a consultation paper to consult on the rules governing the loss-absorbing capacity requirements applicable to authorized institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing the loss-absorbing capacity of authorized institutions helps reduce the likelihood of a financial crisis and thereby benefits society, it also inevitably entails costs. Box 5 provides a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of the loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that the implementation of the loss-absorbing capacity requirements would bring net benefits to the Hong Kong economy.  As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of Category 1 institutions rose from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable for 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions edged down slightly from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorized institutions indicates that the Hong Kong banking sector is able to withstand liquidity shocks arising from possible fund outflows from Hong Kong.  Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio  The Net Stable Funding Ratio, as one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. This requirement aims to reduce banks' medium- to long-term funding risks by requiring them to set aside sufficient stable funding sources to finance their business activities. Specifically, Category 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of not less than 100% at all times.57  Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of December 2017, customer deposits accounted for 56.2% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, broadly the same as six months earlier (Chart 5.8).  Chart 5.8 Liability structure of all authorized institutions  The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 77.1% at the end of June 2017 to 82.7% at the end of December (Chart 5.9), reflecting that Hong Kong dollar loans and advances grew faster than deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined from 65.5% at the end of June 2017 to 63.1% at the end of December. Overall, the all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio rose from 71.4% six months earlier to 73.0%. Banks should assess the impact of the rising loan-to-deposit ratio on their liquidity management. We estimate that, under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200 basis point rise in interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base at the end of December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nevertheless, in view of the expected continued interest rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve and the commencement of its balance sheet normalisation, banks should assess the impact of this situation on their interest rate risk management.  Chart 5.10 Impact of interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks  In the second half of 2017, amid a moderate but still favourable economic environment, the growth in total loans and advances of all authorized institutions slowed from the strong growth of 10.2% recorded in the first half to 5.3%. After two years of decelerating growth, total loans grew robustly by 16.1% for 2017 as a whole. The asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At the end of December 2017, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorized institutions declined to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, compared with 0.84% and 0.61% respectively at the end of June. For retail banks, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio also declined to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth of loans used outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks' asset quality may be more sensitive to the external environment, and therefore banks should closely monitor their credit risk. The HKMA's December 2017 Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook showed that 29% of the responding authorized institutions expected loan demand to grow in the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A).  The credit risk of personal loans remained low during the review period. Banks' mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying at a low level of 0.03% at the end of December 2017. The average loan-to-value ratio of newly approved mortgages fell further from 50.1% in the second quarter of 2017 to 48.8% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.12).
