To counter the potentially severe economic shock that the epidemic may cause, some central banks (including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England) have cut interest rates since early March, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets still face immense sell-off pressure, leading to a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which may in turn intensify the downside pressure on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index. Apart from the development of the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also loom over the global economic outlook. In particular, with regard to trade tensions, although policy risks have declined following the conclusion of the "Phase One" trade agreement between China and the United States, subsequent negotiations may prove arduous as there remain many thorny structural issues to be resolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the European Union and the United Kingdom are not expected to proceed smoothly, thereby prolonging the uncertainties in the aftermath of Brexit. In addition, oil prices have plunged sharply since March, which will exert pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained weak in the second half of 2019 owing to sluggish global demand. Exports from the East Asian region to various major destinations, such as the United States, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there were preliminary signs that the downcycle in technology products in the region was bottoming out and rebounding—including reports from large electronics companies in the region of improved earnings at the end of 2019⁶—whether there is a genuine rebound in the region's technology product exports remains to be seen. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise exports to major destinations. Persistently weak economic growth and trade uncertainties have also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital investment in most East Asian economies declining in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which in the long run may affect the region's potential economic growth. In order to support economic growth in an environment of moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines and South Korea, after cutting interest rates in the first half of 2019, lowered their policy rates again in the second half, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross fixed capital formation. The coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that economies in the region may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As a number of economies in the region have imposed entry and exit restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism industry has borne the brunt, with economies more reliant on Mainland Chinese tourists and tourism service exports being more severely affected by this epidemic (Chart 2.7). The persistence and intensification of the epidemic will also affect supply chains in the region that are closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism exports and Chinese tourists. In the near term, this epidemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these effects may be transient, but the actual situation will depend on the severity of the epidemic, the extent of its spread and whether government actions to contain the outbreak are effective. At the same time, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although the market expects corporate earnings to deteriorate in the near term (Chart 2.8), loose global monetary conditions have encouraged yield-seeking activity, thereby pushing up asset prices in the absence of fundamental support. As a result, the region's stock markets are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected earnings of constituent stocks of benchmark equity indices. Second, the weakness in corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for private institutions in the region to repay their debts. Although declining local interest rates can provide breathing room for indebted companies and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. In addition, as described in Box 1, when more index-tracking funds flow into the region's financial markets, the risk of debt overhang among private institutions may also intensify, although this effect may be confined to enterprises with more solid financial foundations and their long-term borrowings. Third, in terms of external factors, the risks faced by East Asian economies may also increase in the face of an increasingly hardline protectionist US trade policy. Despite the recent progress in the "Phase One" trade agreement between China and the United States, trade tensions between the two countries persist as the fundamental trade issues between them remain unresolved. As evidenced by the continuous increase in the trade surpluses of a number of economies in the region with the United States (Chart 2.9), multinational corporations may continue to seek additional supply channels beyond China-centric supply chains in order to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging Asian economies (excluding China) with the United States had risen to about US$167 billion. If the trade surpluses with the United States continue to widen, the relevant Asian economies may become the next targets of the trade war; for example, the US government imposed tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019.⁷ In view of this, despite the China–US trade truce, the region's trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Merchandise trade surplus with the United States. Over the past decade, the intensifying integration of international financial markets has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds.⁸ Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly referred to as passive funds), but also funds that are actively managed with reference to investment indices.⁹ By bringing in overseas investors that the relevant economies would otherwise be unable to attract or reach, these funds help promote the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. Consequently, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, contributing to the long-term growth and stability of the markets. But is there really no such thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, the market is concerned that investment by such funds may weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers in which they invest, thereby resulting in high leverage levels of the relevant enterprises.¹⁰ In addition, some argue that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has intensified the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, rendering emerging market economies—already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors—even more vulnerable.¹¹ This Box assesses the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Based on the weights of the constituent bonds within the benchmark index, passive bond funds allocate their investment funds to the relevant bonds. Therefore, relative to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may leave the issuers of the index constituent bonds lacking the incentive to act in the interests of the fund investors.¹³ Worse still, from the perspective of financial stability, such behaviour may encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and solvency risks to the corporate sector of emerging market economies, whose leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies. Using the weights of enterprises in various emerging market economies within a mainstream index tracking emerging market economy corporate bonds as an estimate of the extent to which their bonds are invested in by passive bond funds,¹⁴ we find that an increase in such investment would push up the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratios of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated effects. In addition to promoting the development of the corporate bond markets in emerging market economies, the long-term bond investor base expanded by passive bond funds is also conducive to the development of enterprises in emerging market economies. We also find that the aforementioned effect has a significant impact only on enterprises in emerging market economies with more solid fundamentals (in particular, stronger solvency and lower leverage ratios) (the solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged enterprises or those with weaker solvency appear, on the contrary, not to fall further into a debt trap as a result of investment by passive bond funds. In sum, the above research indicates that the growth of passive bond fund investment may not necessarily substantially increase the solvency risk of the corporate sector in emerging market economies.

Owing to weaker private consumption, reduced investment spending and a lacklustre export performance, the Hong Kong economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, while the coronavirus epidemic has recently added significant downside risks. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the slowdown in global economic growth, US-China trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China, and the development of local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to climb further in 2020. Local inflationary pressure is expected to ease somewhat, though its outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside. The Hong Kong economy contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the contraction in the second half, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the whole year, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since the global financial crisis in 2009.  Figure 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components  On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed markedly in the second half (Figure 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell successively by 0.4%, 3.0% and 0.3% in the second, third and fourth quarters, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. On the domestic front, private consumption was the main factor dragging down GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activity, and the economic outlook consequently weakened and dampened consumer confidence, so private consumption contracted significantly from the third quarter. 33 Owing to increased economic uncertainties and deteriorating business sentiment, total investment spending remained weak and dragged down GDP in the fourth quarter. 34 On the external front, with the intensification of US-China trade frictions, weakening global economic growth and a sharp drop in the number of visitors to Hong Kong, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish (Figure 3.2). 35 Under the impact of the sharp contraction in exports of services, net exports dragged down GDP in the third quarter, but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance.  Figure 3.2 Real imports and exports  Given the substantial headwinds facing the economy, the Government rolled out several rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to relieve the financial burden on the public, safeguard employment, and support enterprises, in particular small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and the hardest-hit sectors such as retail, catering services, transport and tourism. 36 To give banks more room to step up their support for the local economy and to help smooth out the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that it would lower the banks' countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity to enterprises, including SMEs. Hong Kong's economic performance in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, while the epidemic has recently added significant downside risks. As some sectors had yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the epidemic would deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget could provide assistance to households and enterprises (especially SMEs), including the distribution of a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and the provision of a special concessionary low-interest loan with a 100% government guarantee to enterprises under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme". 37 On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further lowered banks' countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.0% to 1.0%, which would give banks more room to step up their support for the local economy, in particular the sectors and individuals coming under greater pressure in the short term due to the impact of the epidemic. Analysed by GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak owing to fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively sluggish as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the phase-one US-China trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to disruptions in regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-border economic activity (such as tourism), thereby limiting Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2020 will range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast of international institutions and private-sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is affected by the numerous uncertainties and risks described in the preceding chapters. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Figure 3.3). Among them, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation and food services sector rose to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe blow caused by the social incidents. 39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. Among them, the decline in employment mainly came from the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services and construction industries. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in view of the aforementioned weak economic outlook, the labour market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is very likely to climb further. Box 3 will explore the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market in greater detail.  Figure 3.3 Labour market conditions  Local inflationary pressure continued to build up to the third quarter of 2019, mainly owing to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflation momentum also gradually eased. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, and the increase eased slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also softened from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The easing of inflation momentum was due to reduced price pressures on various components of the Consumer Price Index. In terms of traded goods, underlying food inflation remained noticeable owing to rising fresh pork prices, but the price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and durable goods remained mild. In terms of services, as the growth of rents for newly signed private residential leases slowed earlier, the growth of the rental component of the CPI also showed a downward trend (Figure 3.5). Labour cost pressures rose slightly but remained at a mild level in recent quarters (Figure 3.6).  Figure 3.4 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation  Figure 3.5 Rental component of the Composite CPI and market rents  Figure 3.6 Unit labour cost  Local inflationary pressure is expected to ease in the short term. On the domestic front, the weak economic conditions and the widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private residential rents continue to slow, the housing rental component of inflation should ease further. On the external front, imported inflation is expected to remain mild owing to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts that headline inflation in 2020 will range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5% and a headline inflation rate of 1.7%. This inflation outlook is affected by risk factors on both the upside and downside. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economy deteriorates more severely than expected (for example, owing to a prolonged coronavirus epidemic), inflation may be further suppressed. On the other hand, if the disruption to fresh pork supply becomes more severe, it would create upward pressure on inflation. Despite the marked slowdown in Hong Kong's economy, the unemployment rate in the first nine months of 2019 remained at a low level of 2.8-2.9%. It was only as the social incidents persisted that the unemployment rate climbed more noticeably to 3.3% by the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus epidemic, the labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this Box analyses the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market, including exploring why the overall labour market remained largely resilient in the first three quarters of 2019 (with the unemployment rate barely changing), and what implications this has for future developments. This article also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that, partly because adjusting labour demand entails costs, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate tends to lag the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). This lagging nature can explain why the unemployment rate remained low at about 2.9% when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter.  Figure B3.1 Real GDP growth rate and unemployment rate  In terms of labour demand, although the US-China trade tensions and local social incidents dealt heavy blows to employment in the trade and the retail- and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major industries were still able to support the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the financial, business, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the impact of the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained sound, and financial activities in areas such as fintech development and new share offerings were also very active. These factors may all help to support the job market in the financial and business services sectors. In addition, the public administration, social and personal services sectors, including education, health care and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation coefficient analysis shows that, although employment in many industries is highly correlated with real GDP, employment in the public administration, social and personal services sectors is more neutral to the economic cycle. In other words, even if the economy slows, employment in these sectors may not be greatly affected by the cycle.  Figure B3.2 Changes in employment by industry in 2019  In terms of labour supply, the labour force participation rate 40 fell from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against the rise in the unemployment rate. Figure B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped to restrain the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted markedly in the second half, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Taken together, although employment declined during the economic recession, the lower labour force participation rate helped to alleviate the pressure of the rising unemployment rate in the second half of 2019.  Figure B3.3 Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate  Some changes in the structure of the labour market are also worth noting. In particular, the increase in the proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the proportion of self-employed persons and underemployed persons in total employment has declined to 6% and 1% respectively in recent years, while the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second-largest group in the total employed population (about 7% in 2017). 42 Therefore, companies may retain or hire more staff by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that the average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to about 44 hours at present, partly reflecting the greater number of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened from October onwards, with the upward momentum further intensifying in December, keeping the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone over the past few months. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was partly attributable to equity-related demand, and partly due to the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions prompted by the tightening of liquidity approaching year-end. Overall, the Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. Although the coronavirus outbreak affecting market sentiment amid an uncertain external environment could lead to heightened volatility in fund flows, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding the pressure of fund outflows without affecting the city's financial stability. Supported by the increase in equity-related Hong Kong dollar demand (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October onwards (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar intensified further, and from mid-December to February, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate was partly due to buoyant IPO activities, and partly due to the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions prompted by the tightening of liquidity approaching year-end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased somewhat, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar largely followed the movements of the US dollar and edged up slightly during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differentials between Hong Kong and its trading partners were small and thus had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, the movements of the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar largely followed the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. In gauging Hong Kong's fund flows, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts of fund flows: (1) Hong Kong dollar fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. Hong Kong dollar fund flows focus on the currency dimension of fund flows, which helps to assess monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System. On the other hand, cross-border fund flows focus on the movement of funds across geographical regions through the Hong Kong banking system, which helps to assess the stability of Hong Kong's overall financial system. The two concepts of fund flows require different monitoring indicators. In monitoring Hong Kong dollar fund flows, attention needs to be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the Hong Kong dollar will naturally decline, resulting in a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking rate of HK$7.85 to US$1, the HKMA stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars from banks upon request, and the Aggregate Balance will subsequently decrease. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained largely unchanged, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months, so no significant outflow from the Hong Kong dollar was observed during the review period. In monitoring cross-border fund flows, the total bank deposits in Hong Kong are a useful indicator. When there are substantial fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system, bank deposits are bound to decrease. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that there were no significant cross-border fund outflows. The Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner, indicating that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on the city's monetary environment remained limited. Nevertheless, we need to closely monitor the risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak. Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, and the HKMA has the ability, resources, and determination to cope with fund outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Despite the uncertain external environment and a slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained large, rising 4.0% since the end of June to HK$1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained largely unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, as well as government-issued notes and coins in circulation, rose steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base. During the review period, the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply indicators remained largely stable. The Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew 3.5% in the first half of 2019, and subsequently edged up 0.2% over the seven-month period since the end of June 2019. Analysis of the corresponding assets shows that the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 since the end of June mainly reflected an increase in banks' net foreign currency assets, as well as a rise in the Monetary Base (through increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation) (Chart 4.5). Over the seven-month period since the end of June 2019, Hong Kong dollar deposits (the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3) remained largely unchanged (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting the increase in Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its corresponding assets. Over the seven-month period since the end of June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), driven mainly by US dollar deposits, which increased 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits fell 1.0% over the same period, with renminbi deposits recording a slight decline in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions grew steadily by 1.2% since the end of June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong's total broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with total money supply M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since the end of June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related fund demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), the statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency; Chart 4.7 Total broad money supply (M2). Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates were volatile, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand as well as increased capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019, particularly the active IPO activities in the Hong Kong stock market. The Hong Kong dollar overnight interbank interest rate exhibited relatively large fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8).44 During the review period, other short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally rose. The subscription for large IPO listings exerted significant pressure on overnight interbank rates, and Box 4, through empirical analysis, shows that the market's attention to future IPO activities also affected the 3-month Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rate. This situation would arise if market participants estimate in advance the future closing dates of subscriptions for large IPO listings, and prepare medium-term funds ahead of time for early deployment. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates. As for the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it moved downward following the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2019, the yield of the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield of the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond fell by 50 basis points to 1.00% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate, and average lending rate for new mortgages. As for the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. This increase mainly reflected banks' continued raising of preferential deposit rates to attract deposits, thereby pushing up the weighted Hong Kong dollar deposit rate. At the end of October 2019, following the downward adjustment of the target range for the US federal funds rate, a number of retail banks lowered their Prime lending rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, the Prime lending rates of retail banks currently stand in the range of 5.00% to 5.50%. On the mortgage front, for mortgage loans referenced to the Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rate, major banks raised the cap on rates determined by reference to the Prime lending rate, so the average lending rate for new mortgages rose to around 2.63% in October.45 The Prime lending rate in the market has been lowered since November, and the average mortgage lending rate accordingly declined slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak to US economic activity, and to support the US Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Federal Reserve lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0-0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). Although Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates follow US dollar interest rate movements over the long term, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates may be affected by local factors that could influence demand for the Hong Kong dollar, such as local IPO activities. The Aggregate Balance of the banking system has decreased since April 2018, and the sensitivity of Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates to changes in the supply of and demand for Hong Kong dollar funds may have increased. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance level of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet the needs of interbank payment settlement. In fact, Hong Kong's interbank market has been operating in an orderly manner. Should liquidity become tight in the short term, banks may make use of the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. In view of the possible escalation of the China-US trade conflict, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi against the US dollar falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Entering October, amid market expectations of a resumption of China-US trade talks, the renminbi's depreciation trend reversed, and the offshore and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter, and after China and the US signed the phase-one trade agreement, at one point broke through the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020. However, since the end of January, due to the coronavirus outbreak, the offshore and onshore renminbi again came under pressure to weaken. The offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi for most of the period from May to August, and largely at a premium later in 2019, with the discount briefly widening at the end of January 2020, but the spread between the two remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates. Despite the volatility in the renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained largely stable. During the review period, the 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank interest rate continued to hover between 3-4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank interest rate experienced brief fluctuations in late August and late November due to the MSCI (Morgan Stanley Capital International) A-share adjustments, and again at the end of January 2020 as the Lunar New Year holiday approached.

Amid increased uncertainties in the global and local economic environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and robust by international standards. Asset quality remained at a healthy level by historical standards. Although the growth rate of total loans slowed somewhat in the second half of last year, it still outpaced the growth of deposits over the same period during the review period. Correspondingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions in all currencies, as well as the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio, both rose. However, given that the Aggregate Balance of the banking system remained at a stable level and deposits remained largely steady, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future course of China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify.  In the second half of 2019, the overall pre-tax operating profit⁵⁹ of retail banks fell slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Correspondingly, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than the 1.23% recorded in the same period of 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), the net interest income of retail banks continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, both loan impairment provisions and operating expenses of retail banks increased, resulting in a slight decline in profitability. Chart 5.1 Retail bank profitability. Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks.  Although the US federal funds target rate was lowered three times by 25 basis points each in the second half of 2019, the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market has not yet experienced significant downward pressure to date. On the contrary, affected by a number of local factors (including seasonal demand for funds, increased liquidity demand due to large initial public offerings, and tighter liquidity conditions in the interbank market), short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. Meanwhile, during the review period, longer-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained largely stable, with the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate staying at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to the level six months earlier (the blue line in Chart 5.3). At the retail level, as the Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rate remained close to zero, retail banks had limited room to follow suit in cutting rates after the US lowered its policy rate.⁶⁰ On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete to attract long-term stable deposit funding.⁶¹ Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) gradually rose from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% at the end of 2019, though it remained at a relatively low level by historical standards (the green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates.  From a more comprehensive perspective, given that the decline in the US dollar funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong offset the slight rise in their Hong Kong dollar funding cost, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks' net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding costs, as well as the relatively high level of Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates, providing support for the banking sector's profitability over the same period. Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks. Note 1: Since June 2019, all licensed banks required to comply with the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks continue to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding cost and maturity have been calculated as a weighted average of the relevant figures for these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards cannot be directly compared with figures for previous months.  Looking ahead, a number of downside risk factors in the external and local environment will continue to cast a shadow over banks' profit outlook. Relevant factors include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of China-US trade relations, and the intensification of geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could dampen already-weak global economic growth momentum and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low interest rate environment may persist, which could put pressure on banks' future net interest margins. At the local level, the local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to weigh on business investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or even intensifies further in the future, it could worsen the outlook for credit demand and the asset quality of banks. In terms of overall market developments, following the granting of eight virtual banking licences by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking sector has begun to launch virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market share by launching more convenient products and offering more attractive deposit rates to attract new customers, this could put upward pressure on the funding costs of existing banks. Although the short-term impact may remain moderate given the currently limited business scale of virtual banks, its long-term impact may depend on whether existing banks accelerate the adoption of financial technology to maintain their competitiveness. The results of Box 5 show that the extent to which Hong Kong banks adopt financial technology is statistically correlated with improvements in their cost efficiency and enhancements in their profitability levels.  The capital base of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above the minimum international standards. As at the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions rose further to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capital base of locally incorporated authorized institutions. In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, there is also the non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement under Basel III, which is used to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, exceeding the statutory minimum level of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions.  Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio⁶⁵ requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also rose moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio. The Net Stable Funding Ratio,⁶⁶ as one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicates that the funding position of authorized institutions is stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75% applicable in 2019. The ample liquidity and robust funding position of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is able to withstand a variety of liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio.  Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2019, the proportion of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained largely unchanged, edging down from 56.4% six months earlier to 56.3% (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions. The average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 89.3% at the end of June 2019 to 90.3% at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.10), owing to the fact that the level of Hong Kong dollar loans and advances remained largely stable while deposits declined slightly during the review period.⁶⁷ Meanwhile, as the growth of foreign currency loans outpaced that of deposits, the average foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio also rose from 58.9% to 60.4% over the same period. Overall, the average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions in all currencies rose from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% at the end of the same year. Given that the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has remained stable since April 2019 and that deposits have remained largely steady, there were no clear signs of significant outflows of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system during the review period. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions.  The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2019. We estimate that, under the assumed shock of a 200 basis point rise in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks.  Against the backdrop of tense China-US trade relations, a global economic slowdown, and ongoing local social incidents, bank credit growth slowed in the second half of 2019 after a moderate rebound in the first half of the year. On a half-yearly basis, loan growth (as measured by the change in the total loans and advances of all authorized institutions) grew moderately by 4.2% in the first half of 2019, before slowing to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was attributable to the fact that the growth of both domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and loans for use outside Hong Kong showed a slowing trend during the review period. Domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2% respectively in the second half of 2019, lower than the 4.5% and 3.5% growth in the first half. Nevertheless, the total loan growth for the whole of 2019 still rose moderately to 6.7%, higher than the 4.4% recorded for the whole of 2018.

The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines has brought hope for reopening economies, boosting the outlook for global growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets have repeatedly hit new highs. Nevertheless, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery across economies is expected to be uneven. Over the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, high debt levels, and the long-lasting economic scars caused by the pandemic will be the challenges facing policymakers going forward. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, mainly driven by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no sign of a large-scale outflow of funds from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting weak economic activity and reduced credit demand amid the recurring pandemic, the banking sector's total loans declined slightly in the second half of the year, yet still recorded a mild increase for 2020 as a whole. At the same time, the residential property market was largely stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties over the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic weakens the repayment ability of businesses and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of related downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but with COVID-19 infection numbers rising again from the fourth quarter, global growth slowed once more. Nevertheless, following the breakthrough in vaccine development at the end of 2020, markets expect the pandemic to eventually end, which would help the global economy return to normal and accelerate growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, even though signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the outlook for the global economy. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. At the same time, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing policies could lead to higher-than-expected inflation, which in turn could require central banks to reduce monetary easing earlier, ending markets' expectations of a "lower-for-longer" monetary policy. Over the long term, policymakers will need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures, and address the numerous economic legacies triggered by the pandemic, including high global debt levels and long-lasting economic scars. In East Asia, supported by a rebound in export demand, gross domestic product growth improved in the second half of 2020. With increased risk appetite, portfolio investment inflows into the region rebounded and search-for-yield activity re-emerged. Despite the aforementioned positive developments, East Asia still faces persistent uncertainties brought about by the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, less developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and services sectors. Second, uncertainties may arise regarding the supply, coverage, or effectiveness of vaccines, and combined with weakening fiscal positions of governments in the region, this could worsen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of capital flows. As for Mainland China, as consumption activity gradually returned to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook still largely depends on the development of the pandemic and changes in US-China tensions. The latest consensus forecast indicates that the Mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi recorded several months of depreciation in early 2020, and subsequently strengthened for the remainder of the year as economic recovery accelerated, the US dollar weakened, and the Mainland bond market recorded strong capital inflows. Detailed studies show that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamental factors rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving renminbi exchange rate movements (for details, please refer to Feature 1). Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real gross domestic product remained well below pre-pandemic levels. With a slight increase in local demand and further expansion of goods exports, seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product began to rebound in the third quarter, ending the previous five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real gross domestic product also narrowed markedly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to about 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real gross domestic product fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and marked the first time in history that two consecutive years of decline were recorded, following the 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest data on gross domestic product by industry show that the contraction in consumption- and tourism-related sectors was worse than the overall economy under the pandemic. To respond to the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two further rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020, to help sectors and citizens affected by the pandemic and to strengthen Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capacity. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures to boost the economy in the recent 2021/22 Budget, including the issuance of a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and the provision of 100% guaranteed special personal loans for the unemployed. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced the extension of the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme" to October of the same year, and announced the extension of the repayment period for trade financing loans under the scheme. These deferral measures are expected to help ease the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. COVID-19 vaccines are expected to help economic activity return to normal, and the local economy is expected to resume positive growth in 2021 (for the year as a whole), but the strength and pace of the economic recovery will be affected by numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination takes time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. On external factors, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, which could provide support for Hong Kong's goods and services exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes. The Government forecasts real gross domestic product growth of between 3.5% and 5.5% in 2021, while the average growth forecast by international institutions and private-sector analysts is 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate climbed further, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS epidemic. To respond to the continuously deteriorating labour market conditions, the Government launched the "Employment Support Scheme" under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing employers with time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to help them retain employees. After the "Employment Support Scheme" ended, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off subsidies) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support the sectors hardest hit by the pandemic. In the short term, owing to weak economic conditions, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure. Feature 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to weaken over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell markedly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further declined to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, although fluctuating slightly in recent months, also remained at a relatively low level. As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, Hong Kong's inflationary pressures may remain mild in the short term, and in particular, local inflation will continue to be restrained by the earlier slowdown in the growth of newly signed private residential rents. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation of a moderate 1.4% for 2021, while the Government forecasts underlying and overall inflation of 1.0% and 1.6% respectively for 2021. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, mainly driven by equity-related demand for funds, including from buoyant IPO fundraising activities and southbound inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar on the strong side. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with inflows into the Hong Kong dollar reaching HK$263.3 billion. The strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times over 2020 as a whole, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. From a geographical perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no sign of a large-scale outflow of funds from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued US-China tensions may intensify volatility in capital flows, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and is therefore able to withstand fluctuations in capital flows. As the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking increased the Aggregate Balance, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally remained at extremely low levels. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. Owing to lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. As the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate strengthened, the offshore renminbi (CNH) has appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium relative to the onshore renminbi exchange rate, with the average premium in the fourth quarter at about 100 pips, which is still moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit rising to RMB826.3 billion as of the end of January 2021. As for other renminbi businesses, renminbi bank loans in Hong Kong decreased, while renminbi trade settlement grew, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level of RMB1,191.5 billion over 2020 as a whole. Hong Kong has an efficient financial infrastructure that provides investors with numerous cross-border fund flow channels connecting to the Mainland. As the Mainland's capital account continues to open up, international investors' demand for renminbi assets increases, and regional economic and financial cooperation deepens under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Supported by rising global stock markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by Mainland investors through the Stock Connect (Southbound Trading), the local stock market rebounded after a substantial correction at the beginning of the review period. Global stock markets rose for reasons including unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies; market optimism over positive progress in vaccine development, which could help accelerate the recovery of economic activity; and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered its losses after a sharp decline in 2020, rising 15.1% during the review period, and at one point in mid-February 2021 broke through the 31,000-point mark, hitting a 32-month high. Supported by stable issuance volumes, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. After substantial net fund outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence recovered rapidly as governments around the world rolled out unprecedented economic stimulus measures, and bond funds flowing into the local market rebounded. Although bond yields rebounded moderately over the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, still hovered near historic lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, the market expected that the COVID-19 pandemic would eventually end and that the global economy would subsequently accelerate its growth. Coupled with the anticipation of a "lower for longer" global monetary policy, investors were undeterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021. However, the fervent expectations of financial markets have become disconnected from the still-challenging macroeconomic environment. Should the strength of the economic recovery fall short of expectations, or should policy support be withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for example, due to higher-than-expected inflation), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers will face the difficult question of when to withdraw policy support, as well as the challenge of addressing the many problems left behind by the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and long-lasting economic scarring. Persistent uncertainties surrounding the pandemic continue to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, where the region's slower-developing emerging market economies may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in the progress of vaccination programmes could reverse the current optimistic sentiment, making capital inflows and financial markets unstable.  As for Mainland China, with consumption activity gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking ahead, the outlook for economic growth remains fraught with uncertainty and will depend largely on the development of the pandemic and changes in US–China tensions. Accordingly, the government announced that it would continue to maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasised the importance of controlling systemic risk.  Benefiting from the purchasing power unleashed by economic reopening, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, COVID-19 infection numbers have climbed again, prompting governments in various jurisdictions to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, once again weakening global growth momentum. At the end of 2020, a more transmissible variant of the virus emerged and subsequently spread around the world, making the situation even more severe. Nonetheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use at the end of 2020, the market expected the pandemic to eventually end and the global economy to return to normal and accelerate its growth. Another force underpinning the global economic recovery came from continued policy stimulus, including major central banks' commitment to a "lower for longer" monetary policy amid subdued inflation, as well as sustained fiscal easing in major advanced economies—particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Correspondingly, in January 2021 the International Monetary Fund (IMF) revised its forecast for 2021 global GDP growth upward to 5.5%, 0.3 percentage points higher than the forecast made in October 2020 (Chart 2.1).  Chart 2.1 IMF real GDP growth forecasts made in January 2021 and October 2020  Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, and share prices in cyclical sectors—which typically benefit from economic recovery—rose, driving global share prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2).  Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major stock indices  However, while financial markets performed strongly, the macroeconomic situation remained challenging, and the disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets amid multiple risks. First, the prospect of the pandemic being brought under control depends on whether vaccines can be widely distributed, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate was still low (Chart 2.3). Although global mechanisms (such as COVAX) promote more equitable vaccine distribution, given the limited vaccine supply, the problem of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies is expected to be more severe. If the pandemic is not brought under control as hoped, various jurisdictions may need to extend social distancing and other restrictive measures, thereby dampening the prospects for global recovery.  Chart 2.3 Proportion of the population having received at least one dose of vaccine in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021)  Second, the rebound in financial markets is built on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, especially the "lower for longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures could be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, driven by the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong money and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have already heated up (Chart 2.4). If inflation turns out stronger than expected in the future, central banks may need to scale back monetary easing, and higher-than-expected inflation data could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets.  Chart 2.4 US and euro area 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates  Third, there is significant uncertainty surrounding the future of US–China relations. The wave of US–China "decoupling," particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hardline stance of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the US towards Mainland China, this trend may not be reversed under the Biden administration. An unexpected escalation of US–China tensions could trigger turmoil in financial markets in the future.  Looking ahead, policymakers will need to confront the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. Although premature withdrawal of such measures could jeopardise the economic recovery and create a "cliff effect," in the long run these measures are costly, including imposing fiscal burdens and delaying the necessary post-pandemic reallocation of resources—for example, by allowing "zombie firms" whose business models are no longer viable to survive on continued government support. In addition, policymakers must also address the many problems left behind by the pandemic. First, owing to declining corporate revenues and surging government spending, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 (Chart 2.5). Although the problems posed by the surge in debt may not be imminent given that global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, the continued accumulation of debt in both public and private sectors could give rise to market concerns over fiscal sustainability and financial stability.  Chart 2.5 Global debt as a proportion of GDP  Another lingering problem concerns the potential long-term economic losses or lasting scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, elevated uncertainty could lead firms to reduce investment, while workers plagued by long-term unemployment may permanently exit the labour market, resulting in a substantial waste of human resources.  In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after a sharp decline in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The momentum for economic recovery came mainly from a rebound in exports, among which demand for exports of electronics and technology equipment was strongest. At the same time, the hardest-hit service sectors (such as tourism and consumer services requiring face-to-face contact with customers) continued to struggle.  Chart 2.6 East Asia: 2020 real GDP growth  Despite the uncertainties still surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment funds have flowed back in. Since the second half of last year, owing to improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to advanced economy bonds, the region has attracted greater inflows of bond funds (Chart 2.7). As signs of economic recovery emerged and vaccine production programmes were rolled out, equity funds also flowed into East Asia at an accelerated pace in the final quarter of 2020. Regional currencies also appreciated accordingly as a result of the portfolio fund inflows, causing the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index to rebound by about 10% from its low in March of last year.  Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment fund flows  East Asia continues to face persistent uncertainties from the pandemic. First, although the rollout of vaccines has brought hope to the region's hardest-hit service sectors and economies, competition around the world for early vaccine batches has driven up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution also poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capacity. As a result, the region's slower-developing economies may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of travel-related sectors. Second, since investors' optimism has been driven largely by the vaccine rollout, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination falls far short of expectations, the current capital inflows and the rebound in financial asset prices could come to an end. A sharp reduction in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turmoil.  With COVID-19 successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovering, the Mainland economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical supplies and high-tech products), exports also maintained growth (Chart 2.8). Over the course of 2020, despite the unprecedented shock the economy suffered under the COVID-19 pandemic, Mainland GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%.  Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contributions of demand components to GDP growth  Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecasts indicate that the Mainland economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to become the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economic recovery can be sustained still depends to some extent on the development of the pandemic. Although industrial production activity on the Mainland has normalised, the service sector continues to face some disruption as the pandemic re-emerged in several northern provinces. In terms of the external environment, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain owing to a new wave of the pandemic in most advanced economies. In addition, US–China tensions may not ease in the short term, but the earlier signing of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the concluded China–EU Comprehensive Agreement on Investment (CAI), on which agreement had been reached, could help China integrate further with other economies, potentially offsetting part of the adverse impact of US–China decoupling on the economic recovery. Given the continued uncertainty in the economic outlook, at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 the government announced that there would be no major change in the existing policy stance in 2021, in order to support economic growth, while also emphasising the importance of controlling systemic risk—for example, maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. In the long run, the "14th Five-Year Plan" has designated technological self-reliance and the "dual circulation" strategy as priority development directions, with the aim of raising per capita GDP to the level of a moderately developed country by 2035.  The COVID-19 outbreak appears to have had little impact on the repayment capacity of bond-issuing enterprises, and the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remained relatively low in the second half of 2020. However, owing to a sharp increase in defaults on state-owned enterprise bonds, the total amount of defaulted bonds in 2020 rose (Chart 2.9). Although the rise in state-owned enterprise defaults mainly reflects the central government's determination to break the "rigid redemption" of state-owned enterprises in order to promote more rational market pricing of risk, the limited fiscal space of some local governments may also be a contributing factor, particularly the local governments of less developed regions.
