Although the continued economic recovery and the gradual normalisation of interest rates contributed to some extent to the rise in financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate default events in the final quarter of 2020 caused credit spreads to widen significantly (Chart 2.10).  Chart 2.10 Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields  In the real estate market, Mainland housing prices continued to rise in the second half of 2020, especially in first-tier cities. By contrast, housing prices in lower-tier cities rose at a much slower pace (Chart 2.11). As for the housing oversupply problem that had plagued third-tier cities in previous years, it was largely brought under control in 2020, partly because third-tier cities recorded strong sales amid buoyant market sentiment. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities stood at around 13 months, well below the peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) remained well below its pre-pandemic level, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 as local demand recovered and merchandise exports expanded further. With the prospect that COVID-19 vaccination would bring economic activity back to normal, the local economy is expected to return to growth in 2021 following its most severe contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given the time required for widespread vaccination, the local economy will still face considerable challenges in early 2021. As such, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while local inflationary pressure should stay mild. The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remained well below its pre-outbreak level. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and narrowed further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. Nonetheless, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and marked the first-ever two consecutive years of decline in history following the 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest data on GDP by industry also showed that economic activity in the vast majority of sectors recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with the consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracting more sharply than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter comparison, real GDP began to rebound from the third quarter of 2020, ending the preceding five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Local private consumption returned to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters; however, amid the local third and fourth waves of the pandemic, the authorities reimposed social distancing measures, and consumer confidence remained weak. As the business sentiment improved briefly, overall investment expenditure also grew in the second half of the year. Partly benefiting from stronger export performance (particularly exports to Mainland China), Hong Kong's merchandise trade expanded further (Chart 3.2). As global tourism remained at a standstill, services trade stayed weak. Overall, net imports (trade deficit) weighed on GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting the slower recovery of merchandise exports relative to imports. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components; Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports. In response to the ongoing pandemic, the government rolled out two further rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund totalling HK$30.4 billion between September and December 2020, to help sectors and citizens affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's capacity to combat the epidemic. In the recent 2021/22 Budget, the government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures to boost the economy, including the disbursement of a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and the provision of a 100% guaranteed personal concessionary loan for the unemployed. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, announced that the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme" would be extended again to October of the same year, and announced an extension of the repayment period for trade financing loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help ease the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines expected to bring economic activity back to normal, the Hong Kong economy is projected to resume positive growth in 2021 (for the year as a whole), but the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given the time required for widespread vaccination, the local economy will still face considerable challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, which could provide support for Hong Kong's merchandise and services exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes, thereby affecting Hong Kong's merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The government forecasts real GDP growth of between 3.5% and 5.5% for 2021 as a whole, while the average growth forecast of international institutions and private-sector analysts is 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and the early part of 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, a 17-year high (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also climbed to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. Total employment stabilised after falling to a low level (Chart 3.3), while government figures showed that the number of job vacancies continued to decline. The nominal average wage index for employed persons, which reflects labour income, slowed to 2.0% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. In response to the continuously deteriorating labour market conditions, the government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing employers with time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to help them retain their employees. After the Employment Support Scheme ended, the government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off subsidies) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support the sectors hardest hit by the pandemic. In the near term, given the weak economic conditions, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure. Feature 2 examines the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions; Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation. Local inflationary pressure continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell markedly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further declined to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively (Chart 3.4). The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects the momentum of inflation, fluctuated slightly in recent months but also stayed at a relatively low level. Specifically, price pressures on basic food items eased somewhat, and the cost of dining out declined notably, reflecting more restaurants offering takeaway discounts amid restrictions on dine-in services. Price pressures on other traded goods (such as durables) remained moderate. On the services side, as private residential rentals consolidated, the rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index remained soft (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures have also eased in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.5 Rental component of the Composite CPI and market rentals; Chart 3.6 Unit labour costs. As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, local inflationary pressure should stay mild in the near term. In particular, affected by the slower growth in newly signed private residential rentals earlier, local inflation will continue to be restrained. The market consensus forecasts headline inflation of a mild 1.4% in 2021, while the government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 1% and a headline inflation rate of 1.6% for 2021. With the COVID-19 pandemic raging, inbound tourism rapidly fell into a slump, and the market is concerned that this crisis will have scarring effects on the recovery of the labour market going forward. To this end, this feature empirically analyses the impact of the boom in inbound tourism on Hong Kong's labour market, in order to explore the potential effects of the current tourism slump. Since 2000, inbound tourism has experienced significant ups and downs (Chart B2.1). Specifically, the number of visitor arrivals to Hong Kong declined during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in 2003. Following the launch of the "Individual Visit Scheme" (individual travel) in July of that year, visitor numbers began to surge. Under the initial Individual Visit Scheme, Mainland residents could apply on an individual basis for one to two trips to Hong Kong per year, with each stay not exceeding 7 days. The scheme was expanded from April 2009, allowing eligible residents holding Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple-entry "Individual Visit" endorsements to Hong Kong within a year (multiple-entry permit). Since then, the number of Mainland visitors has increased substantially. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure connecting with Mainland China, the number of visitor arrivals to Hong Kong reached a record high in late 2018 to early 2019. The subsequent local social incidents halved visitor numbers in the second half of 2019, and under the COVID-19 pandemic, inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies. We use the tourism boom brought about by the Individual Visit Scheme as an example to examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and income. We consider the Individual Visit Scheme launched in 2003 to be akin to a random economic shock, as it was nearly exogenous in timing and could not be anticipated by Hong Kong citizens. Our main analytical data come from population data in Hong Kong's Population Census or By-census. Specifically, we use the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Census or By-census. In addition, we define tourism-related industries as the catering, retail, hotel and transport industries. First, we adopt the "difference-in-differences" method as an analytical framework, comparing the difference in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme between younger workers (aged 20-40) belonging to the "treatment group" and older workers (aged 41-65) belonging to the "comparison group". We classify the younger cohort into the "treatment group" because they are still at the early stage of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. Since the impact of the tourism boom brought about by the Individual Visit Scheme on the labour market may change over time, we also adopt the "event study" method to identify effects that vary over time. Our empirical findings show that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers (especially women and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism-related industries after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme. Among them, the impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on the probability of young women engaging in tourism-related industries was particularly significant and persistent, remaining at close to 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards (in terms of the average difference in entry probability relative to the older cohort) (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar method to compare the income of those engaged in tourism-related industries (treatment group) with those in non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). The estimation results show that, after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme, the income growth of workers engaged in tourism-related industries was higher than that of employees in non-tourism-related industries. Moreover, compared with similar employees in other industries, female workers and workers with lower educational attainment employed in tourism-related industries saw higher income increases with an upward trend (3-20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on female employment; Chart B2.3 Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on the income of women and workers with lower educational attainment. The above results are broadly consistent with international experience, revealing that tourism is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women and workers with lower educational attainment. In the case of Hong Kong, our findings are also consistent with those of previous analyses, namely that the strong growth of inbound tourism increased market demand for lower-skilled workers and improved the robustness of the labour market for lower-skilled workers. As inbound tourism falls from boom to trough, these worker groups may be more affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to trade close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, which was triggered multiple times during September to October 2020. The strong demand for Hong Kong dollars was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that arising from buoyant initial public offering (IPO) fundraising activities, as well as southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) declined across the board. Although uncertainties related to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and the ongoing tensions in Sino-US relations may intensify capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and has the capacity to withstand the pressures brought about by capital flow volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that arising from buoyant IPO fundraising activities, as well as southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some funds raised from IPOs were remitted away, owing to the improved sentiment in the local stock market and market expectations of rising funding demand towards the end of the year, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate stayed within a narrow range of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December. As fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the Aggregate Balance, reflecting substantial capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. From September to October 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times. In accordance with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). Over the whole of 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times, with cumulative inflows totalling HK$383.5 billion. Analysed from a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating that there was no sign of substantial capital outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that direct investment by non-residents continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, without showing any abnormal capital movements. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX); Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. During the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar declined broadly in line with the softening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and had a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, the movement of the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and the ongoing tensions in Sino-US relations may intensify capital flow volatility. As an international financial centre, various fundraising activities (such as IPO fundraising) take place in Hong Kong, resulting in substantial capital inflows into and outflows from Hong Kong. On the one hand, such fundraising activities can attract international investors to move funds into Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business needs. Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, and has the capacity to withstand capital flow volatility without affecting financial stability. Amid continuous capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. In the eight months since the end of June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). Analysed by component, the increase in the Monetary Base during this period reflected the increase in the Aggregate Balance arising from the multiple triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking. On the other hand, other components, including the Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base. During the review period, large-scale IPO fundraising activities increased the Hong Kong dollar deposits derived from IPO subscription loans, so the Hong Kong dollar broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component rose significantly during July to October 2020 and January 2021 (Chart 4.6). As IPO fundraising activities ended and customers repaid IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. Entering January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 again increased substantially, mainly driven by large-scale IPO fundraising activities at the end of January. Overall, over the seven-month period since the end of June, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7%, and excluding the impact of the IPO fundraising activities at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew moderately by 9.1%. Analysed by counterpart assets, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 was mainly due to the increase in the Monetary Base driven by the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (Chart 4.7). As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period, and excluding the impact of the IPO fundraising activities at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits recorded a decline due to low deposit rates, this was fully offset by the rapid growth in demand and savings deposits driven partly by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency; Chart 4.7 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and counterpart assets. Total foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven-month period since the end of June. US dollar deposits edged down 0.3%, partly reflecting the weak US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting the increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, as IPO fundraising activities caused short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits, total deposits with authorized institutions rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the IPO fundraising activities at the end of January, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that, as the monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), the statistics should be interpreted with care. As the Aggregate Balance increased, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates remained at extremely low levels overall during the review period (Chart 4.8). Although there were large-scale IPO fundraising activities in the second half of 2020, due to the ample liquidity in the banking system, HIBORs did not fluctuate substantially. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates. The Hong Kong dollar yield curve broadly tracked the movement of the US dollar yield curve and steepened during the review period, with short-term bond yields falling and long-term bond yields rising (Chart 4.9). Compared with the end of June, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds edged down 4 basis points to 0.23% at the end of February, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose 67 basis points over the same period to 1.30%. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate, and average lending rate for new mortgages. At the retail level, Hong Kong dollar interest rates mainly declined in line with the Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, further declined from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% at the end of February 2021 (Chart 4.9). Owing to lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking the movement of the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rate of retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the prolonged low US interest rates, Hong Kong dollar interest rates should continue to remain at low levels, with occasional fluctuations due to capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. Faced with a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, the ample liquidity in the banking system should provide a sufficient buffer to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar have strengthened since the end of May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting the better economic outlook of Mainland China relative to the rest of the world, as well as the weak US dollar. After FTSE Russell announced at the end of September that Mainland government bonds would be included in the World Government Bond Index, investment demand further supported the strengthening of the renminbi. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium relative to the onshore renminbi exchange rate, with an average premium of about 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates. During the review period, the liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate fluctuated briefly due to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand towards the end of the year, it remained below 4% most of the time (Chart 4.11). The 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate declined in late December in line with onshore renminbi interest rates, and subsequently rose again in late January, partly due to tightening onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate fixings. In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued its growth trend. Since the fourth quarter, the growth of renminbi deposits has accelerated, partly reflecting the appreciation of the renminbi and the relatively higher interest rates on the renminbi compared with other currencies. Relative to the end of June 2020, the growth of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit outstanding accelerated, reaching RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among these, renminbi customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by the strong growth in corporate customer deposits. On the other hand, the outstanding certificates of deposit decreased by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong. As for other renminbi business, over the seven-month period since the end of June 2020, the outstanding renminbi loans declined by 2.4% to RMB159.2 billion. On the other hand, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. During the seven-month period from July 2020 to January 2021, the transaction amount handled by local banks reached RMB3,769.5 billion, an increase of 16.7% compared with the same period a year earlier. Among the relevant transactions, the growth in remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland was higher than the growth in remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong possesses a large renminbi liquidity pool, sufficient to continue supporting a substantial volume of renminbi payments and financial transactions. Over the whole of 2020, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system reached as high as RMB1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Amid the persistent economic recession caused by recurring waves of the COVID-19 pandemic, and coupled with the impact of a prolonged low interest rate environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined further in the second half of 2020, while asset quality also deteriorated slightly. Nevertheless, given their still-strong capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, in order to continue supporting the overall economy through difficult times, the HKMA decided to extend a number of relief measures. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic will be brought under control and economic activity can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. The aforementioned uncertainties and ongoing geopolitical tensions would be unfavourable to business activities and continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic would weaken the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of the relevant downside risk factors on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets dropped to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared with 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), causing net interest income to decline by an amount that outweighed the slight increase in non-interest income, resulting in a drop in profitability. For 2020 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, and the return on assets declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Retail bank profitability. Chart 5.2 Retail banks' net interest margin. Largely due to the substantial inflow of funds driven by stock market activities, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more ample. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). The composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) followed a broadly similar trend, dropping notably from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (the green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected the lower interbank funding costs and the reduction in time deposit interest rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates. From a broader perspective, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks. Looking ahead, as the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks' net interest margin performance, the profitability outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging. Moreover, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have strengthened market optimism about the global economic outlook, given the considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain. The aforementioned risk factors will continue to affect the loan quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term. The capital position of Hong Kong's banking sector remained robust and well above the minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, higher than the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). During the period, the Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7%, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a sound level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum level of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capital position of locally incorporated authorized institutions. Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions. As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio. The most recent ratio figures under the Net Stable Funding Ratio requirement also indicated a stable funding position of authorized institutions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions were maintained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75% respectively. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicated that Hong Kong's banking sector is able to withstand liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remained the primary funding source of authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure maintained in the banking system. At the end of 2020, customer deposits accounted for 56.1% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, similar to the level six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions. As the total deposits of all authorized institutions increased in the second half of 2020 while total loans decreased over the same period, the average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions for all currencies fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% at the end of 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits largely reflected growth in both their Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, as at the end of 2020, the average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio dropped to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively, compared with 86.4% and 65.5% respectively six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions. The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained relatively low in the fourth quarter of 2020. Under an assumed shock of a 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks was estimated to be equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks. Against the backdrop of a persistent economic recession caused by recurring waves of the pandemic and tightened social distancing measures, total loans and advances registered a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. However, for 2020 as a whole, total bank credit still recorded positive growth, though its growth pace slowed markedly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, the total loans and advances of all authorized institutions decreased by 1.8% in the second half of the year, following growth of 3.0% in the first half of 2020 (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was attributable to decreases in both domestic lending (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. In particular, total domestic lending edged down by 0.9% in the second half of the year, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with growth of 2.6% and 4.2% respectively in the preceding six months. Chart 5.12 Loan growth. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans, after decreasing by 2.0% in the first half of the year, remained broadly at a level similar to that at the end of June by the end of 2020. Foreign currency loans, after growing substantially by 10.6% in the first half of 2020, decreased by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a decline in demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector's outlook for short-term credit demand was slightly more optimistic than six months earlier. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2020 showed that the proportion of surveyed authorized institutions expecting an increase in loan demand over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting a decrease in loan demand over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). As the pandemic adversely affected the repayment ability of households and companies, banks' loan quality deteriorated slightly, but remained sound by historical and international standards. In addition, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. The total specifically classified loan ratio of all authorized institutions edged up from 0.79% six months earlier to 0.9% at the end of 2020, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions rose from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% at the end of 2020. The novel coronavirus pandemic caused a huge shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open-ended funds experienced large capital outflows (Chart B1.1), placing pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Capital outflows from some open-ended funds during the March 2020 event. Apart from investors' liquidity needs, another reason for the large capital outflows may be that investors took advantage of the "first-mover advantage" to redeem their funds early, thereby avoiding bearing redemption costs that may surge under market stress. To curb capital outflows caused by the first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds adopt swing pricing — an open-ended fund pricing rule that reduces investors' first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this event, there has been no empirical research indicating whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this backdrop, this box conducts an empirical study to understand whether swing pricing was able to reduce capital outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 event, thereby lowering their liquidity risk. In addition, this box also seeks to identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we put forward policy recommendations regarding financial stability. The first-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of other investors, thereby passing the redemption costs on to them. The first-mover advantage exists mainly in open-ended funds that adopt traditional pricing rules, where the subscription and redemption costs of the fund's investors (such as the trading costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-ended fund price after the transactions are conducted. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem their shares first do not have to bear such trading costs. This becomes an incentive for them to redeem their funds early, especially when large redemption costs are anticipated. Therefore, during periods of market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced due to the expected rise in redemption costs. This amplifies the redemption pressure and liquidity risk faced by open-ended funds.

During the review period, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained accommodative. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base rose by 1.4% over the eight months since the end of June 2021, driven mainly by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting the additional issuance of notes to meet banks' sustained demand for Exchange Fund Bills amid ample liquidity in the banking system, the outstanding amount of Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, while the Aggregate Balance (before Discount Window activities) correspondingly decreased by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued notes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, total deposits with authorized institutions grew moderately by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits rose slightly by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics may be subject to volatility caused by various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, and business- and investment-related activities), and it is therefore advisable to observe longer-term trends. For the whole of 2021, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits grew by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency. Overall, transactions in Hong Kong's interbank market continued to be smooth and orderly. As liquidity in the banking system was ample, HIBOR continued to stay low despite market concerns over US monetary tightening (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting market expectations of rising funding demand towards the year-end, HIBOR edged up slightly in December 2021. The average lending rate for newly approved mortgage loans rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample liquidity in the banking system can provide a sufficient buffer during large-scale capital market activities or financial market volatility. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates. During the review period, the offshore renminbi interbank market continued to function normally. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand towards the year-end, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (CNH HIBOR) experienced slight fluctuations in late December 2021, while the 3-month CNH HIBOR remained relatively stable and hovered around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Overnight and 3-month CNH HIBOR fixings. In the second half of 2021, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow steadily. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, the balance of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew by 30.3%, reaching RMB1,113.5 billion at the end of January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Among these, renminbi customer deposits increased by 33.5%, driven mainly by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in the balance of certificates of deposit. Chart 4.9 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong. Over the six months since July 2021, although the outstanding amount of renminbi loans decreased by 10.2% to RMB167.6 billion, Hong Kong's renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. Between the end of July 2021 and the end of January 2022, the transaction volume handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,763.0 billion (Chart 4.10), an increase of 18.3% from RMB3,181.0 billion in the same period a year earlier. Hong Kong's sizeable renminbi liquidity pool continued to support a large volume of renminbi payment and financing transactions. For the whole of 2021, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system rose from RMB1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB1,522.6 billion. Chart 4.10 Renminbi trade settlement remittances. Looking ahead, with the establishment of the two-way southbound and northbound Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening up of the Mainland's capital account, growing international investor demand for renminbi assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Major global stock markets continued to rise in the fourth quarter of 2021, but have consolidated since January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalating conflict between Russia and Ukraine. The Hong Kong stock market remained sluggish in the fourth quarter of 2021, weighed down mainly by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties surrounding the development of the pandemic in Hong Kong caused the Hang Seng Index to fall to a nearly two-year low at the end of February. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi bond market continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly affected by weakening asset market sentiment and a new local wave of the pandemic. Major global stock markets generally continued to rise in the last quarter of 2021, leading the MSCI World Index to hit a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022 (Chart 4.11). Supported by government monetary and fiscal stimulus, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings underpinned the upward trend of major global stock markets, but the pandemic remained investors' major risk concern throughout the year. However, major global stock markets have consolidated since early January 2022, amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies against surging inflation risks, sharply rising commodity prices, and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. By contrast, the Hong Kong stock market continued to lag behind other major global stock markets at the end of 2021. The Hang Seng Index hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November, and closed at 23,398 points at the end of 2021, down 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, buying interest from value investors returned to the Hong Kong stock market, pushing the Hang Seng Index back up to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties surrounding the development of the pandemic in Hong Kong and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the Hang Seng Index down to a nearly two-year low of 22,713 points at the end of February. Over the entire review period from the end of August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index fell by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index fell by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11 Hang Seng Index and MSCI World Index. Owing to the emergence of the highly contagious Omicron variant, stock market implied volatility fluctuated sharply at the end of November 2021 before subsequently easing. Although the skew index retreated from its record high in late June 2021, it remained at a high level, reflecting investors' concerns about a correction in the prolonged stock market rally since the outbreak of the pandemic, and their willingness to invest more funds to hedge against downside risks in the stock market (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Option-implied volatilities of the Hang Seng Index and the S&P 500 Index, and the skew index. Against the backdrop of ample global liquidity, the Hong Kong stock market has continued to record net inflows of international investor funds since the last report (Chart 4.13). By contrast, the southbound Stock Connect recorded significant net fund outflows in the third quarter of 2021, mainly due to concerns over the impact of Mainland regulatory changes on technology stocks. However, buying through the southbound Stock Connect began to recover in December 2021, recording total fund inflows of HK$98.3 billion by the end of February. During the review period, the cumulative net buying amount increased by 5.7% to HK$2,233.0 billion (Chart 4.14). Chart 4.13 Net fund inflows into Hong Kong's stock market. Chart 4.14 Net flows through the Stock Connect scheme. After Hong Kong's primary market raised a record high amount of funds in the first half of 2021, activity slowed in the second half. For the whole of 2021, there were a total of 98 new share listings, raising a combined HK$328.9 billion (Chart 4.15), with total fund-raising down 17.8% from the previous year. In 2021, HKEX ranked fourth in the global IPO market, behind Nasdaq, the New York Stock Exchange, and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15 Hong Kong's IPO market. The outlook for the local stock market remains uncertain. The easing of the Mainland's monetary policy and more Chinese concept stocks conducting secondary listings in Hong Kong's primary market will improve sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market. However, the stock market still faces many headwinds, including uncertainties surrounding the development of the local pandemic, a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined in the second half of 2021. The specified classified loan ratio edged up slightly in the second half of 2021, but remained low by both historical and international standards. Supported by robust capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, in order to further help the economy weather difficult times, the HKMA extended a number of support measures. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the economic recovery, coupled with the risk that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation could be faster than expected—both of which will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should stay vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 16.1% compared with the same period in 2020. The weak profitability was mainly attributable to a decline in net interest and non-interest income as well as an increase in operating expenses. As a result, the return on assets fell to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.1). For 2021 as a whole, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared with 2020, while the return on assets dropped from 0.77% to 0.59%. Chart 5.1 Retail Banks' Profitability Reflecting the continued impact of the low interest rate environment, the net interest margin of retail banks also remained at a low level of 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Retail Banks' Net Interest Margin Reflecting year-end funding demand and the decline in the Aggregate Balance following the HKMA's additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) recorded a slight increase in the final quarter of 2021. However, as liquidity in the banking system remained very ample, interbank rates continued to stay at relatively low levels. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR rose slightly by 9 basis points from six months earlier to 0.26% at end-December 2021 (see the blue line in Chart 5.3). The funding costs of retail banks remained stable during the review period. Among them, the composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) rose moderately by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months earlier to 0.21% at end-2021 (the green line in Chart 5.3). From a broader perspective, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong rose slightly by 6 basis points in the second half of 2021 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Although the normalisation of US monetary policy may signal an improvement in banks' profitability, any near-term improvement may be partly offset by two factors. First, although the Federal Reserve has indicated that it will raise interest rates multiple times in 2022, past experience shows that changes in local interest rates may lag behind US rates (particularly when interbank liquidity in Hong Kong remains very ample). Therefore, an improvement in banks' net interest margins may take more time to materialise. In addition, the surge in Omicron variant cases may also introduce uncertainty into the pace of economic recovery, thereby exerting pressure on banks' asset quality and profitability. The capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.2% at end-2021 (Chart 5.5), well above the international minimum requirement of 8%. The Tier 1 capital ratio and the Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio during the period were 18.2% and 16.2% respectively. Climate change affects every aspect of our lives, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impact. In this regard, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has devoted substantial work to advancing Hong Kong's climate goals and to enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following last year's inclusion of our first sustainability report as a chapter in the HKMA Annual Report 2021, this year we have published a standalone Sustainability Report 2022 for the first time. I hope this report will give readers a deeper understanding of the HKMA's work strategies and priorities in strengthening the Hong Kong banking system's capacity to respond to climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and how we put into practice our roles as a responsible investor and a sustainable organisation. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability efforts across the HKMA's major functions. In this report, you will learn about our specific measures and work, with the following being some of the key highlights: Banks face climate risks in their day-to-day operations. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete measures to strengthen banks' capacity to respond to climate change. In 2022, we developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the supervisory process, and studied how to harness the power of technology to help banks assess the impact of physical risks. In view of the growing number of green and sustainable products launched by banks, we also shared with the industry good practices on how to properly manage these products, so as to enhance banks' capacity in climate risk management. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives on addressing climate risks and promoting the development of sustainable finance. On the local front, we are working with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (the Steering Group) to develop a local green classification framework; the framework will increase transparency in the financial market and promote greater consistency in green finance policies. At the international level, we are actively participating in a number of different international organisations to help formulate policies to address climate change and to assess its impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well positioned to meet Asia's demand for green and sustainable financing. Although 2022 was a rather challenging year for global bond markets, Hong Kong's green and sustainable debt issuance continued to record strong growth, rising by 42% to a total issuance of US$80.5 billion, making Hong Kong the largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuance in Asia². The relevant issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government and the Hainan Provincial People's Government, whose issuances once again demonstrated Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable funds between the Mainland and international markets. The vibrant development of Hong Kong's green bond market can also be partly attributed to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing green bonds totalling nearly US$16 billion, with the proceeds raised allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, and energy efficiency and conservation. We also helped the Government achieve two "firsts", including assisting the Government in issuing its first batch of government green retail bonds totalling HK$20 billion in May 2022, which was the largest green retail bond issuance in the world at the time. In addition, we assisted the Government in issuing its first batch of tokenised green bonds in February 2023. This was the world's first batch of tokenised green bonds issued by a government, and the issuance also marked a milestone as it successfully combined our strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and financial technology. Standards, data and talent are indispensable elements for the sound development of the climate finance ecosystem, and can only be established through the efforts and collaboration of different sectors. To this end, the HKMA works mainly through the Steering Group with other relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions and the financial industry to develop the above elements. In addition to developing the local green classification framework mentioned above, the Steering Group has also, through the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance established under it, promoted skills training in the industry and improved Hong Kong's data resources. Furthermore, the Steering Group has made good progress in other areas such as mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund's work on responsible investment, in particular by setting a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. At the same time, we also enhanced our risk management work to improve the Exchange Fund's climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns. In addition, to fully capture the opportunities that climate change may bring, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment for the Exchange Fund by seeking out investment opportunities that help support climate transition and mitigate climate change, so as to enhance the long-term returns of the portfolio. At the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio had fallen by 43% from the 2017 level. In fact, the Exchange Fund's exposure to high-carbon assets has continued to be lower than that of the overall market. Going forward, we will continue to advance towards the net-zero emissions target by continuously strengthening the integration of environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, actively exercising our ownership rights as an asset owner, continuing to collaborate with various stakeholders, and focusing on the decarbonisation and transition of the portfolio. Within the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA's sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is built on three pillars: the environment, staff and social responsibility. On the environmental front, we are committed to promoting a green working environment and advocating a more environmentally friendly market to the public; on the staff front, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthy and inclusive working environment; and on the social responsibility front, we are committed to enhancing the public's level of financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion, and actively giving back to the community. Compared with the levels when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and paper usage in 2022 all achieved double-digit reductions. More importantly, we have established a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the short term, our target is to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions and, using 2015 as the baseline, to reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 or earlier. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require the continuous efforts and collaboration of many parties. On this important global issue, we understand that we must take concrete action and lead by example, and work together with like-minded peers and international organisations. In the next section, we will outline the HKMA's short-term plans and work priorities in addressing climate change under each of its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a formidable task, and we will spare no effort in achieving this goal. We are confident that, with the concerted efforts of all our colleagues, the financial industry and the public, we will be able to successfully meet the climate challenges of the future. Eddie Yue, Chief Executive

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong's financial industry, and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and a sustainable organisation. At the same time, through participating in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the regulator of the banking industry, we will endeavour to strengthen the climate resilience of the banking sector and further improve our green finance ecosystem to support banks' green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will communicate with banks to understand their progress in implementing the supervisory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review process, and revise the banking industry's "Green Baseline" common assessment framework. At the same time, the HKMA will support banks in their efforts to enhance their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, for example by exploring various measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, measure and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also work with banks to launch the next round of climate risk stress test exercise as part of the supervisor-driven periodic stress tests for 2023 to 2024. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to cope with climate risks based on an enhanced stress test framework; the framework covers various stress scenarios such as extreme climate conditions and adverse economic environments. To foster the healthy development of banks in offering green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on the sales process in a timely manner. We will also conduct off-site thematic reviews to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to strengthen the building of a green finance ecosystem to support the green transition of the financial industry, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements for developing a local green taxonomy framework. On market development, to promote Hong Kong as a green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA will assist the Government in expanding the issuance scale of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and broadening the scope of the programme to cover sustainability bonds; at the same time, it will attract more green financing activities to be conducted in Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA will also help implement the Government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Training Scheme to expand Hong Kong's talent pool in green finance. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of integrating green finance with technology. On the other hand, we will continue to work with other institutions and departments through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group on cross-sectoral topics such as skills training and data, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA will jointly launch various dedicated programmes with the International Finance Corporation in the Asian region, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, as well as providing practical guidance to help banks formulate roadmaps to develop green finance into a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme to expand the Alliance's influence in the Asian region. At the same time, the Alliance will also strengthen the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, promote green finance knowledge sharing, and lead the launch of projects in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set the target of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio by 2050 or earlier, as its commitment to participating in global climate response efforts and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social and governance factors into its investment management process, strive towards the target of net-zero emissions, and fully support global climate response efforts. As a responsible and sustainable organisation, the HKMA cares about its staff, the general public and the surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations, as our commitment to participating in global decarbonisation and climate response efforts. The HKMA will continue to give priority to reducing carbon emissions and encourage staff to give their full support in saving energy and reducing waste. In addition, we will provide further guidance to staff on incorporating sustainability principles into the procurement process. To achieve digital transformation and enhance operational agility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise its internal systems and applications to further improve work efficiency, while minimising as far as possible the potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change is a significant risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong's financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong's climate goals as well as the global sustainable development agenda. In their day-to-day business operations, banks are exposed to the impacts of various sustainability and climate-related issues. To continue to perform their important functions in the financial system and to channel more funding towards green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA places particular emphasis on building banks' capabilities to respond to and manage climate risks, and on accelerating banks' efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes, and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife smuggling. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)¹ published the Principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks, and responded to frequently asked questions to clarify how the existing Basel framework covers the aforementioned risks. In response to these international developments, the HKMA will continue its efforts to incorporate climate-related factors into the regulatory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" in 2021, the HKMA has maintained communication with banks to exchange views on the expectations, progress and challenges in implementing the relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks' climate risk management, the HKMA has developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the banking supervisory process, and communicated this to the banking industry in June. As part of the implementation of the two-year plan, the HKMA issued a revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1 "Risk-based Supervisory Approach", and enhanced the CAMEL² rating system by incorporating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. At the same time, drawing on the experience gained from the 2021 pilot exercise, the HKMA has refined the climate risk stress test scenarios and assessment framework. The HKMA has also developed a plan to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress testing into the regular supervisor-driven stress testing, so as to conduct a more comprehensive assessment of the banking industry's resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues (including climate risk management and transition planning). At the same time, the HKMA is reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks' capital adequacy levels and to determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with the aim of encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address the risks related to climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. In view of the growing popularity of green and sustainable products issued by banks, the HKMA conducted a thematic review, primarily examining banks' development and ongoing management of these products. During the thematic review, the HKMA identified a number of good practices and issued a circular in December to share these with the industry, encouraging banks to progressively strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. Applying technology can enhance data availability and strengthen banks' capabilities to manage climate risks. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. In addition, the HKMA, together with other central banks and regulators, completed a project under the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Network to explore how technological solutions can assist in conducting physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and world-leading anti-money laundering practices; this work employs advanced analytics and compliance technology (Regtech), complemented by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the anti-money laundering regulatory data collection process to reduce banks' manual workload and paper consumption. To enhance transparency across financial markets and to bring greater consistency to green finance policies, the HKMA is collaborating with other financial regulators to develop a local green classification framework. A green classification framework, commonly referred to as a green taxonomy, categorises economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has maintained contact with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to explore in depth the features and challenges of the framework, and is preparing to make recommendations and conduct a consultation on the structure and core elements of the framework in the first half of 2023. The HKMA is keenly aware that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, and has therefore incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to strengthen its ongoing monitoring efforts. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks, and has incorporated analysis of climate-related risks into its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Workstream under the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA has helped to further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and supervisors to gain a clearer understanding of the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. In terms of research work, the HKMA carried out a number of applied research projects in 2022, exploring in depth two major topics, namely greenwashing behaviour in the corporate green bond market³, and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposure⁴. The above research findings help to inform the formulation of policies and regulatory measures to address the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Locally, this research helps to strengthen the HKMA's ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared its research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research seminars and the HKMA's Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA's Liquidity Facilities Framework is a collateralised standby liquidity arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is studying the incorporation of sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, the HKMA helps to facilitate international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability, and draws insights from it to help strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong's financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong's position as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA has stepped up its efforts to raise market awareness and participation, provide the necessary infrastructure and enablers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Cross-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance (the Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the financial industry's response to climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the Government's climate strategy1. The Steering Group's work is primarily modelled on its strategic plan, which sets out six focus areas and five action points to consolidate Hong Kong's financial ecosystem and jointly build a greener and more sustainable future (Chart 1). Strengthening climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong's position as a global risk management centre; promoting the flow of climate-related information across all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation and investor protection; enhancing the relevant skills of industry practitioners and raising public attention and awareness; encouraging product innovation and research initiatives to steer capital flows towards green and sustainable projects; seizing the business opportunities brought by the Mainland and developing Hong Kong into a green finance centre of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (the Greater Bay Area); and strengthening regional and international cooperation. Actions taken to date to advance the development of sustainable finance in Hong Kong: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. The Steering Group's current work priorities include skills training and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), the green taxonomy (see the section "Building a Green Taxonomy Framework to Facilitate Green Fund Financing" under the chapter "Building a Sustainable Financial System" on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, as well as carbon market opportunities. Specifically, in March the Steering Group published a preliminary feasibility assessment of Hong Kong's carbon market opportunities and will support Hong Kong's development into a regional carbon trading centre, including developing an international high-quality voluntary carbon market and seizing the opportunities brought by Greater Bay Area cooperation. In December, the Steering Group announced a partnership with CDP2 to enhance data availability in Hong Kong and strengthen sustainability reporting. As part of this collaboration, the two parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting non-listed companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which not only facilitates companies in conducting sustainability reporting but also assists financial institutions in collecting and analysing company-level data for use in risk assessment and related business decisions. This marks an important step in the Steering Group's efforts to expand the coverage of its data work to include SMEs, an important economic segment that has previously been relatively difficult to reach. The Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance in July 2021 to coordinate the work of financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders and academic institutions on training and policy formulation, and to build a resources and data repository. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three information repositories dedicated respectively to data, training information and internship opportunities, helping the financial industry and other sectors gain access to green and sustainable finance-related data and learning resources. The resource repository provides data sources for assessing Hong Kong's physical risks. To help the industry cultivate talent, the Centre in December assisted the Government in launching the "Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Training Scheme", providing subsidies to practitioners, students and graduates who participate in green and sustainable finance-related training and skills enhancement. Other measures to promote skills training include the launch of the "Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative" to create more internship opportunities for students, and the development of a new "Green and Sustainable Finance" module3 under the HKMA's "Enhanced Competency Framework" for banking practitioners. "Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Training Scheme" The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the "Alliance for Green Commercial Banks"4, bringing together financial institutions, banking industry organisations, research institutions and innovative technology providers in the region to jointly develop a collaboration platform for green commercial banks. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to realise their full potential, develop green finance into a mainstream core business, and promote the financial system's participation in global climate change-related activities.
